RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. OWD PUDDLER'S MEET. Owd Puddler's signed teetotal. He's done t' saine oft afoor, But this time he's i' earnest —Ate, sweeazs he'll spree no moon.. , , - Ile mopes abeawt so ooletui, Wl' grim face, long an' sad, An' tells h's mates i' whispers A tale abeawt th' Owd Lad!

He'd bin on t' slotch a fortnut, An' rolled hooam every neet Weel looaded up wi' penky, Mekkin Wa o deftwn t' street His nooase hed getten fiery As onny signal lamp, An' be wur co'd bi th' nayburs A nasty drunken scamp.

He fairly bed his hand in At kekin up pint pots; He'd popt, an' spent, an' borrowed, An' owed some daycent " shots." When t' lads i' th' fowd up yonder, Agreed to play a trick, Thro' them,—he's signed teetotal, Thro' them,—he's sin Owd Nick!

Dan Dibbles, in a raffle, Hed won a billy-gooat, A reglar smart owd tupper ; So, when it coom to t' vacate, 0 t' lads resolved to use id, An' mek id act tha.d fleet For th' benefit Fuddler, To cure a slotch wi' freet.

lleet coom an o wur ready I' t' darkest nook o' t' fowd ; Th.y'd t' gooat hid in a hoss rug, For th' wind wur blowin' cowd ; When Fuddler, drunk as usual, Zigzagged on t' scene ; An' th' Ids brunt Bengal matches, Some red 'uns, an' some green.

'Twur late, an' nobry sturrin', No seawnd, but th' wind, wur heeard ; When Fuddler see th' leets brunnin', Be pood up—gradely feared.. Then o went dark o' th' sudden, An' grooans o reawnd him rooase ; Then summat roared like thunder. An' Fuddlees marro' frooaze !

He grooaped his way reawnd t' corner, When reet afoor his een He see a shinia' monster Stood in a flame o' green; Wi' horns, an' cloven feet too, An' een as red as ire ; One look med Fuddler's yure stick up As stiff as copper wire.

An' off he flew like leetenin', A gradely sowbered mon • He'll keep eawt ov his clutches, He says, while'er he con; Say nowt to him o'er t' matches. Th' phosphorus, born or th' gooat, Or else he'll start o' An' pop his Sunda' cooat. JAI* o'

- - "We don't sell spirits," said a law-evading beerseller. "We will give you a glass, and then if you want a biscuit we'll sell it to you for threepence. The "good creature" was handed down a stiff glass and swallowed it, and the landlord handed his customer a biscuit. • "Well, no, I think not," said the customer, "you sell 'em too dear. I can get lots of 'em five or six for a penny elsewhere." You may live simple, manly lives, speaking your own thought, paying your own way, and doing your own work, whatever that may be. You will remain gentle- men as lon e as you follow these rules, if you have to sweep a crossing for your livelihood.' You will not re- main gentlemen in anything but the name if you depart from them, though you may be set to govern a kingdom. —Thomas Hughes. A well-known French traveller, on his return from Fiji, happened to call on the late Baron James de Roths- child, and the latter—always on the lookout for informa- tion—pre,sed him for matters of interest concerning that country. After much hesitation, the visitor at leneth remarked that what had struck him most was that there were no Jews and no pigs whatever on the island. " Let us go there together. dear boy," quickly answered the baron ;" "we shall make a fortune." LORD Demme AN RODERS.—Lord Dudley, receiving a visit from the poet Rogers at Paris, proposed that they should go together to the Catacombs. It has often been remarked of Rogers that with his fine bald head, wrinkled akin, and sunk cheeks, he was more like a death's head than any man that was ever seen alive. Accordingly, when the poet had spent an hour or two in the abodes of mortality, and was about to make his exit, the keeper, startled at his death-like appearance, tried to stop him, crying out: " Hulloh! Get you hack! You have no right to come out !" Rogers afterwards comnlained to Lord Dudley that he had cruelly deserted him in this emergency. "My dear Rol:ere," replied the Earl, "I did not like to interfere, you looked so much' at home." TURPENTUCTL—After a housekeeper fully realises the - --Worth of turpentine in the household, she is never will- ing to be without a supply of it. It gives quick relief • burns; it is an excellent application for corns; it is good for rheumatism and sore throats, and it is the quickest remedy for convulsions or fits. Then it is a • sure preventive against moths; by just. dropping a trifle In the bottom of drawers, chests, and cupboards, it will render the garments secure from injury during the sum- mer. It will keep ants and bugs from closets and store- rooms, by patting a few drops in the corners and upon the shelves; it is sure destruction to bedbugs, and will effectually drive them away from their haunts if thoroughly applied to the joints of the bedstead in the spring cleaning time, and injures neither furniture nor clothing. A spoonful of it added to a pail of warm water is excellent for cleaning paint. A little in the suds on washing days lightens laundry labour. Kiss Let(o) Tux DARIC—On one of the seats of an American train was a married lady with a little daugh- ter ; facing them was another child, a son, and a coloured "lady" with a baby. 'rhe mother of these children was a beautiful matron, with sparkling eyes, in exuberant health and vivacious spirits. Neer her sat a young : lieutenant, dressed to kill, and seeking a victim. He scraped up an acquaintance with the mother by atten- tions to the children. It was not lone before he was essaying to make himself very agreeable to her, and by the time the sun began to decline one would have thought they were old familiar friends. By and by the train approached a tunnel. The gay lieutenant leaned over and whispered something in the lady's ear. It was noticed that her eyes flamed immediately with indigna- tion. A moment more and a smile lighted up her features. The smile was not one of pleasure, but was sinister. It was unperceived by the lieutenant Into the tunnel ran the train: The -lady and the coloured nurse quickly exchanged seats. The gay lieutenant im- mediately threw his arnas round the sable lady, pressed - her cheek to his, and rained fast and furious kisses on her lips. In a few moments the train came out into broad daylight. The white lady looked amazed, the coloured lady bashful, the gay lieutenant befogged. "Jane," iaid the white lady, what have you been doing?" " No- thing," responded the coloured lady. "Yes, you have," said the white lady, not in an undertone, but in a voice that attracted the attention of all in the car. "See how your collar is rumpled and your bonnet smashed !" Jane, poor coloured beautY, hum; herhead for a moment. the "observed of all observers," and then, turning round to the lieutenant, replied, "That man kissed me in the tunnel." Loud and long was the laugh that followed among the passengers. The white lady enjoyed the joke amazingly. The lieutenant looked like a sheep-stealing dog, left the carriage at the next station, and was seen no more. "HURRAH von ETON."—Wellington said that Water- loo was won onehe cricket field of Eton. Ile referred to the gallantry of his officers, many of whom had been trained by the games and sports of that famous school. An illustration of the effect of such training in developing a man's limbs and wind was given at Inker- man, one of the most subbornly fought battles of the Crimean 'Nor :—A young officer who had learned at Eton not much from books, but, a good deal from its sports, had hot work on that eventful night. His sergeant fell at his side. Seizing the dead man's rifle he • fired it, emptied his own revolver, drove his sword through a Russian officer, was surrounded and made prisoner. While going to the rear in charms of two stalwart Russians, he looked at their long coats and said to himself. "They can't run." Watching his opportunity, he knocked one soldier head over heels, threw the other, by a wrestler's trick, into the mud, and tooketo his heels. Before his guardians were on their legs and couldsfire, he had got aver a plod • piece of ground. A Russian lancer made at him; be ran as if leading an Eton foot-race, and cleared a good- sized fence. The lancer cleered it after him, and with lance fixed pressed the fugitive hard. A swollen brook, running fiercely, barred his way. It was seventeen feet wide, but the old Etonian had won the "long jump" when at school, having cleared nineteen feet over Chal- vey ditch. He now jumped the brook; the lancer re- fused to follow, and the young officer ran back into the English lines. "Hurrah for Eton!" he shouted, as a schoolfellow shook his hand—recalling the school where lie had learned to shoot, to fence, the art of boxing, the wrestling dodge, the high jump, the long jump, and the Use of his leg's. SHOCKING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON. On Monday Mr. S. Bright)iv& coroner for South- west Lancashire, held an liftfuest at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-stieet, Warrington, in regard to the death of William Wall (30) a labourer, who was on the previous Friday morning killed by a fall of earth when working at Florence Mills, Howley. The friends of the deceased were represented by Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, and Mr. Ridgway. solicitor, appeared for the owner of tbe Mills, Mr. H. Lees.— Evidence was first given by the mother of the deceased, who said that he had supported her, and by Miss Clarke, a nurse at the Infirmary, who said that deceased was admitted to that institution on Friday, suffering from injuries that resulted in his , death twenty minutes later.—John Featherstone, 14, New-street, Howley, a bricklayer in the employ of Mr. Lees, said that on 'Friday several men were excavating for a water filter at the Florence mills. The work was not being done by a contractor, but by Mr. Lees. Mr. Thomas Fell was the manager of the mills, and it was witness's duty to look after the Men in his absence. On Friday they had just finished excavat- ing when the accident occurred, and the deceased was in :the e'xcavation removing bits of clay, &c., to make the bottom level for the bricklayers to commence work. He was using a spade, when some earth fell from the side on to the deceased, who was covered to the shoulders. . There were three other men in the bottom of the excavation at the time. There were two uprights and one stay between in the excavation. The two uprights were Bft. in length. The deceased was liberated in about three minutes. One man held his head up while two or three others dug away the earth. The ground was wet and marly, and to thathe attributed the accident. One side was propped, the other was not, and the accident occurred on the side which was not propped. Mr. Browne: Is it not the custom in Warring- ton where the excavation is deeper than Bft. to have propping P—Witness : It is a rule if the earth looks loose and dangerous, but this looked solid clay. Further questioned by Mr. Brewne, witness said it was nee a fact that a short time previously a quantity of earth had fallen. No one had asked him to get timber from Mr. Lees. A short time before the man was killed Hickey, one of the workmen, did not request him to ask Mr. Lees to get some timber for propping puzposes.—By Mr, Ridgway: As far as he was able to judge, all proper precautions were taken to prevent accidents.—James , Skelhorn. 19, Orford-street, said he was at Work at the excavation on Friday as a labourer. It was Feather- stone who had control over the propping, as he was the bricklayer. The first stay was, he believed, put in on Thursday morning last, when they had nearly finished ' the excavation. There had been no fall of any moment before the stay was put in. There was plenty of timber on the ground to put up another stay if it was considered necessary. The men working in the hole did not con- sider it neceesary to put up another stay • even the side that fell appeared to be perfectly safe.—John Hickey, a labourer in the employ of Mr. Lees, said he had been working at the excavation. There was a fall on Thurs- day, and it left about two yards of projecting earth, and this fell on Friday, killing the deceased. After the first I fall he asked Featherstone if he was going to have that ' which projected knocked down, as it was not safe for them to work under it. He said "I will see the master in a bit. He will be coming soon, and I will let you. know." Featherstone saw the master in about five or /ten minutes afterwards. Witness also saw Mr. Lees on the top of the excavation. When Mr. Lees had gone away he spoke to Featherstone and asked him what was to be done, and his reply was—" The master says you must not touch it, Get on with your watts and get them hi." The fall took place about five or ten minutes after Featherstone had spoken to him. Witness could get no timber to prop tin the sides without the consent of Featherstone. Before the accident took place, they • spoke to Featherstone about the timber, and lie said there was no:timber to spare, that what tineberthere was was being used.—By Mr. Ridgway There was a lot of ' timber lying about, and some of it nad been used for the stay that was put in.—Mr. Ridgway: If you thought there was danger; why didn't you give up working? —Witness: We should have done so, but a man wants a day's work. If he does not work, another will.—Why did you not speak to Mr. Lees about the necessity for another stay P.—Witness: There was a manager, and we did not like to speak to .he master.—James Maanion, 01d-rd., Latchford, another of the labourers, said that on Friday they made a.complaint to Featherstone that it was not safe to work under the side, and that it should be staved or proppel—The hole should have been tim- bered all round to make it secure.—Featherstone re- called, said the sides were smooth and battered down when the men left work on Thursday night. Ilihen the men went to work at. six o'clock, on Friday mornieg, it was found there had been a slip on one side. The side that fell in was battered from top to bottom. Ile did not ask Mr. Lees or Mr. Fell to supply timber. Neither Mannion, deceased, or Hickey ever spoke to him about danger. They did not ask him for any timber. They did, however, ask him to ask Mr. Lees to look it one quarter which was propped, but which still stood:— I :Henry Ernest Lees, one of the partners of the Florence ' Mill Company, said that Featherstone did not speak to him on Friday morning about the necessity of props being put up, nor did be say that the men had cons plained to him about the existence of a danger.—The Coroner remarked that he thought it would be admitted that Featherstone was the person who had imposed on him the day of seeine that the work was properly carried out. If the master provided the materials and an efficient foreman, he thought he had finished his work. They could not expect a large einployer of labour to have the supervision of every detail; although it appeared that in this case Mr. Leas was anxious to see that every- thing was done that could be done. Featherstone had given his evidence in a very unsatisfactory manner, and it was quite clear he had contradicted himself on many points. It was for the jury to decide whether he was blatneable.—The jury returned a verdict of "accidental death," a'nd added that the negligence of John Feather- stone contributed to the depth of deceased, but only in such a, degree as to render him censurable at their + hands.

A RAILWAY SmAsu.—At midnight on Wednesday a fast goods train, drawn by two engines and running from Sheffield to Manchester, dashed into a standing goods train at Deepcar station, on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Lailway. ,The engine was thrown off the line and greatly damaged; the guard's van and several wagons of the stationary train were smashed and piled high on the track ; but the drivers and guards escaped injury. A dense fog prevailed at the time of the accident. LORD HAIITINGTON AT BELFAST.—Lord HartiTlgtoll, who arrived in Belfast on Thursday, in order to fulfil his engagements with the Ulster Liberal Union Association, was entertained at a banquet in the Ulster Hall last night. Replying to the Mast of his health, he said that in 1885 Mr. Gladstone wrote him a letter on the Irish Question, which made it necessary for him to watch very carefully the public utterances of his leader, and to make ' it clear to the country in what sense he accepted any declarations of Mr. Gladstone upon the subject. Were any credit due tohim in the action he had taken,it was only for encouraging members of the Liberal .party to repudiate the extreme demands which. Mr. Parnell formulated. He contended that the Gladstonian party in Ireland would obtain no support except in so far as Mr. Gladstone was the humble follower of Mr. Parnell. He denied Drat the conditions which he had WEI down ' prevented a constructive policy on the part of the Unionists, and in conclusion said that the time had now come when both sections, Liberal and Conservative, . should combine against the common enemy in order to maintain the Union.

-VISIT OF SANITARY INSPECTORS TO WARRINGTON. On Saturday, a number of the members of the North-Western district of the Association of Public Sanitary Inspectors visited Warrington, and in- quired into the sanitary arrangements of the borough. _Amongst those present were Messrs. T: Dixon ( Wavertree) Chat-inlay of the Association, W. Bland (Barton-upon-Irwell), W. Stanstield (Newton Heatil), Mountfield (Birkenhead), J. Farrington, T. MTarlane, T. Turner. N. Coates, and H. Edwards (Liverpool), Gatton (Litberland), T. Mort (Lymm), A Taylor (Wallasey), G. N. Lloyd (Higher Bebing- ton), T. Proctor (Dalton-in-Furness),W. Hail (Great Crosby), and R. Norman (Warrington). Amongst those who wrote apologies for non-attendance were Dr. Carpenter,,the President of the Association, and 'Dr. Taylor, the vice-President. The visitors arrived ft the Town Hall at about three o'clock in the after- noon, and they were met by Alderman Burgess, Chairman of the Sanitary Committee of the War- rington Town Council, and Mr. T. Longdin, the borough Surveyor of Warrington. In extentling a welcome to them, Alderman Burgess expressed the willingness of the Sanitary Committee to give any information that might be of benefit to the associa- tion. He should be glad to accompany them in any direction they proposed to go, and would assist them in any way that was in his power. Mr. Longdin then briefly explained the system adopted in Warrington for dealing with the refuse of the town. By their system, he said, there was a considerable saving in cartage, for, instead of carting the excreta a mile and a half, they took it to the intercepting depots, where itwas put into tanks, and impelled through pipes to the works at Longford by means of ejectors and compressed air. After the material had been got to Longford, it was put through a process of manufacture, by which it was reduced to a dry powder. This powder found a ready sale among farmers for manure, and, if they had more, they could easily dispose of it. The party then drove to the gas works, where the compressed air is generated by means of Shone's system, thence to the south intercepting depot, and from there to the manufacturing depot at Longford. After a thorough inspection of these places had been made, a visit was paid tothelnfectious Diseases Hospital. Here agreeable comment was made on ;he comfortable and contented appearance of a number of juvenile paients who were suffering from scarlet fever. The wards were found to be spotlessly clean, and exceed- ingly well-or,ered, and Dr. Goma% the medical officer of health, the matron (Miss Walker) and assistants of the hospital, deserve congratulation on the satisfactory state pf affairs there. The disinfecting Ifoom was also inspected. The afternoon's proceedings terminated with the holding of a short meeting at the Patten Arms hotel, where one or two complimentary speeches were made.—Mr. Bland (Barton-upon-Irwell) proposed a vote of thanks to Alderman Burgess for the attention the visitors had received. In Warrington, he said an example had been set that might be extended to almost every town in the country. He thought it was I far better to eject excreta through pipes than to cart it through the district.—The proposition was seconded by Mr. Turner (Liverpool), who remarked that he thought they might safely say that the system they had that 'afternoon witnessed in Warrington was the best system of dealing with excteta. He was particularly struck with the small quantity of plant that seemed to be re- quired, and he was surprised at the information as to how much profit was made out of the sale of the manure. They generally learned that there was a loss on thework- ing of such places.—The motion having been heartily carried, Alderman Burgess, in the course of his reply,' said there was truth in the observation that a:profit was made, but it required explanation. When ,hey had to dispose of the material in its crude condition they could get nothing for it, but under the present system there was an income from the sale of manure, which last year amounted to £2,200. This year, he hoped, it would not be much less than £3,000, although they had had a very great difficulty to contend' with by reason of one of I the dryers having burst. That sum of £2,200 was profit I over and above the system that had been superseded. If they were working on the old system, they would collect at more cost, and would dispose of the material without, in reality, receiving a shilling for it. They made it a fixed rule that filth should have no resting place in the borough of Warringtbn, and they baled to, secure an abundant supply of the most wholesome I water. It was hard and costly, but it was wholesome and there was plenty of it. Then, they tried as far as possible to prevent any undue impurities in the atmosphere, at the same time havingareasonWe regard to the manufacturing interests of thetown. When they had done that, and had attended closely to the over- , crowding that attained in a town like. Warrington, they had done nearly all the work that there was to, be done. It was true the streets required scavenging and watering, but what he had mentioned were the main principles for the guidance of sanitary work. If cleanliness attained from end to end, they had done nearl:v, all that was required.—A vote of thanks was also passed to Mr. Longdin, and, after a similar compliment had been paid to Inspector Norman, the proceedings were brottelt te a conclusion.

div.head: PETROLEUM WELL IN O'FfF,SHIRE.
div.p: A PETROLEUM WELL IN O'FfF,SHIRE.

The reported discovery of a petroleum well: at Anderton, near North wich, is confirmed. The well belongs to the Stanley /Inns Inn, a public-house awned by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, aud Co., Wil- ' derspool Brewery, Warrington, who bought the property some years ago from Lord Stanl'ev of Alderley.. Mr. C. M. Blades, F.C.S., of Northwich, has personally obtained a sample frona the well, and applied to it a few simple tests. He finds that the sample undoubtedly contains petroleum in con- siderable proportions. A. stick immersed in the livid and ishen ignited undergoes a rapid and fierce combustion. The sample emits the unmistakable odour of petroleum, and is in appearance like turbid 'water. Mr. Blades has not yet ascertained the flashing point of it. During his visit' to the well he made a searching inquiry into the possibility of the well having been contaminated from store of petro- leum, but he could find no confirmation of that hypothesis. What renders the existence of petro- leum under the salt beds of mid-Cheshire somewhat probable is the well-attested fact that occasionally salt mines (which as a rule are quite free from inflammable gases) have been the scenes of power- ful though temporary jets of gas which, taking fire from the candles of the miners, obliges them to abandon the mine until the diseharge ceases, A sample of the oil has been sent to Messrs. Greenall and Co.'s head office, and they are, taking steps to have it analysed. The Rural Sanitary Authority 'are making arrangements for extending the water- mains, in order to provide a substitute tor the well. A large quantity of the oil was pumped into the canal before its real character was discovered. For scene time suitableness of the water f er, domestic purposes has been a matter of contention, a local medical man attributing several cases of fatal ill- ness to it, while the analyses of the medical officer of health for the district were held to show that the water was quite fit o drink.

THE MAYOR AND CORPORATION. DINNER AT THE TOWN HALL On Tuesday evening, the Mayor of Warrington :ttlderman Thomas Sutton) entertained the members

of the Town Council, justices of the peace, and the officials of Warrington to a dinner in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall. His Worship presided, and those .preSent were the Rector of w arrington (Rev.. F. W. Willis), Rev. S. Wilkinson (Mayor's
Chaplain) ; Aldermen Burgess, Chandley, Da-vies, Harrison, Holmes, Pickmere, Webster; Councillors
Ashton Illackhurs.t, Bolton, Bakin, Francomli, hem-

ing, Green, E. Greenell, jun., Heaton, Hutchinson, Jolley, Monks, John Piernoint, William Pierpoint,• F. A. Roberts, H. Roberts, J. Taylor. I. V. Taylor, W. Tinsley,Wright • Messrs. W. H. Brook (Town Clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy Town Clerk), C. Clitorley (Borough Treasurer),T. Longdin (Borough Surveyor) W. S. Haddock (Gas Engineer), Robert Pierpoint, J.P., John White J.P., William Owen, John Fair- dough, J. P., Thomas Morris, Dr. S. Smith (police surgeon), Mr. S. Sutton (clerk to the Rural Sanitary Authority), Mr. G. F. F. White (deputpmagistrates' clerk). Letters had been received from the follow- ing gentlemen apologizing for their inability to at- tend :—Lord Winmarleigh, Sir G. Greenall, Bart, M.P., Messrs J. G. McMinnies,Beamont, Peter Stubs, Henry Bleckly, John Rylands, T. G. Rylancls, J. C. Parr, Holbrook Gaskell, E. J. Guest, Charles White. Edward Greene', btc. The catering was entrusted to Mr. and Mrs. T. 0. Speakman, of the Saracen's Head Hotel, Wilderspool, and gave complete satisfaction. The menu was as follows :—Soup: Turtle. Fish: Turbot, lobster sauce, fried sparlings. Entrees: Sweetbreads and peas, mutton cutlets and tematoes. Releves : Boiled capons A la Dubarry, saddle mutton, ham and spinach. Game: Grouse, pheasant, partridge. Entremets : Alex- andra pudding, vanilla cream, ice pudding. Dessert: Grapes, pines, filberts, apples, figs. The vestibule lead- ing into the Council Chamber was tastefully ornamented with plants by Mr. Edward Green, head gardener at Bank Park gardens. After the banquet, The MAYOR proposed the toasts of "The Queen," and "The Prince and Princess of Wales. and the. Royal

Family," which were loyally responded to. Mr. Jour; Winn gave the "The Bishops and clergy, and all minis ers• of religion." For the first time, t.e said, since the new Rector came into residence in War- rington they had his presence at a public dinner when this toast was proposed. There was an old saying, "De mortuis nil ni onum"—" Say nothing but good of the dead "—which might 'with very great propriety be ap- plied to the late Rector, who lived and worked amongst them for over 30 years. He did not think he should be considered unchari, able when he saidthat the late Rector, . .

coming as he did from a London parish of a peculiar nature, never seemed quite to understand the charac- teristics of the Lancashire people. Now, the new Rec- tor, he believed, was Lancashire. born, and though he had lived away from the county for many years, he hoped and trusted he .had not lost his knowledge of Lancashire manners and customs. (Hear, hear.) He thought he might venture te say that if Mr. Willis ful- filled the duties of his high office in a faithful and dili- gent manner, in the manner in which he .I.*ed already led them to believe he would, he would have the hearty co- operation and affection, not only of all Churchmen in the town, but would also gain the esteem and respect of those who belonged to other denominations. (Applause.) With regard to the clergy of Warrington, he felt no hesitationin saying that never in his recolleetion—and he had lived in Warrington all his life—had they had a body of men who had been more zealous and more active in tile discharge of their duties than they had at the present time.. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the great work which the ministers of other denominations did, he had much pleasure in bearing his testimony to it in the matter of civilization and religion.. It was a source of regret they could not all think the same in matters of religion, but they. had the satisfaction of knowing that although they.differed, they agreed to do sp„ and that there was none of that bitterness and animosity and religious clisputer which took place in. days gone by. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Recroe, in. responding!, said he felt encouraged by his belief in the high opinion which he believed, the body which he represented deserved,- and which it received at their bands. With regard to the clergy„he admitted there wata no body Of men who. were perfect, but he did not know any class which hula° few. black sheep. He believedthat if one had tact, consideration, and kindness he could win his way with and though he might no possess these qualities, he hoped he might be able, by the exercise ef good judgment, commonsense real kindness, and love, to win the regard of the people .generally. (Hear, hear, and applause.) With reference ... ()the minis.ers of other bodies, he-had found them to be men of the greatest zeal and earnestness, and he owned some of them as his personal friends. (Applause.), The Rev. S Witatieeme said that reference had been made to the ministers .of other denominations. A short time ago they met at a meeting which was held in the Co-operative Hall, over which the Rector presided,•and there they saw ministers of all denominations.veorking together, and doing their best to lead people into the right way, ,and to promote the cause of temperance. (Applause.) Councillor Moss, in proposing "The Army,. Navy, and Reserve Forces,' said that, as an old Radical with a new face, he lined the present Government at in.y rate would do something towards putting theservice upon what they might consider a proper footing. They had k on the highest authority that they had an army without guns and a navy with ships that would not swim, and if they were-in some naval engagement they would find themselves very well "hammered," as, they used to say at school. With reference to the reserve forces, they might congratulate themselves, ,because after all, they were a very noble body of men; and they had an excellent specimen in' their friend Majov Pick, ram'. (Applause.) Major Picatteee was well received on rising to. res- pond! Governments—both Liberal and Conservative— had„ he said, to a certain extent, behaved well. to the volunteer force, though.ho thought they, ought to go a little further, as he knew that the officers very fre- quently had to dip their hands into their • pockets to assist a force from which the country was reaping a benefit. (Hear, hear.) Alderman DAVIES, in. proposing "the health,, of the Mayer," remarked that his worship had gone. through his year of office with fewer difficulties than most men whoamd preceded him. Some great philosopher had said —and he (Alderman Davies) did not know much about philosophy—" Blessed is the country that has no history, and during the last twelve months they had gone on so peaceably tegether in their deliberations in the Council Chamber that the Mayor had had a very happy time of it—(laugfater)—and he was inclined to believe that that state of things had been brought about by the extraordinary tact of their ' Mayor. He hadd avoided all the rocks and had gone through the duties 1

of offibe very peaceably. and the result i'kas that they had done a great deal of business, although they had made little noise about it. (Laughter and applause.) They gave a hearty recognition to the services of his worship. They wouldsing that he was " A.jally good fellow," and give him three hurrahs that would be welcome to them with their Lancashire ears. They regarded the Mayor very highly, and were quite satisfied with the manner in which he had fulfilled the vary serious and responsible duties of his high office. (Ap- plause.) The toast was received with musical honours; andin reply 'l' he MAYOR said he was proud to occupy the position of Mayor. It had been suggested that he should be i again asked to occu9y the position and he had alrea,dy caomnsliteendt,tbousttahned rein.ustthteelwl tahyemoftahnaytohneadielsden, lotwish for ie knew gendoutbletmwenmainng,thteo aCoonoupnteitlhwe position, were competent, e were and perhaps to some it might seem rather unfair that he should again act aochief magistrate; but his only reason amnadn ny for consenting Ives, this, that he began,to find out that it was only about the- end of the year that a Mayor began to understand his duties, and he had a feeling that he would like to serve again in order to make up for any,short- comings he might have had during hispast year of office. That was the only reason which tempted him to consent to continue in oftee. He could assure them that when he was an errand boy in the office of the first Mayor of War- rington he did not for a moment imagine that he should ever attain to the high position of Mayor of the town and of the chief magistrate of the borough. The church bells rid not at that dine appear to him to say "Turn again, little Sutton, Mayor of Warrington," ' (Laughter and applause.) He was pleased to find that his feeble attempts to perform the duties of the office successfully had to some extent met with their approba- tion. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Alderman BURGESS, in proposing "The member for thb borough," said it appeared to him to be somewhat extraordinary that he, of all those who sat round the table, should have been selected to discharge such a task. He supposed it was well known that for the whole of his political life—for this was a poli ical toast—there had been an antagonism between himself and the mem- ber, which one would have thought. would have pre- cluded him from proposing the toast, but he would endeavour to show them before he sat down how he could possibly be in everything he undertook. (Laughter.) Whatever might have been the antagonism between him and Sir Gilbert:Greenall politically, he was present to say that whoever the inhabitants of Warring- rum chose as their Member in Parliament, he was entitled to all the distinction and to all the honour at the hands of , each one of them that they could give him. (Applause.) While he had differed from Sir Gilbert Greenall through apolitical life—and he expected he ' would do so to the end—still, the respect he entertained for him in his capacity as the representative of the borough was none the less because he happened to bo a , Conservative and he (the speaker) a Liberal. They had • had experiences of that description, as they knew, in their Council Cliambei, and he had never found, although ' gentlemen had differed from him politically—and whom at one time they had striven, to keep, aut of the Council Chamber on political grounds—he had never vet found ; that they were less able or desirious te promote the best interests of the town because they happened to be Con- servatives ; in fact, he had seen amongst some of the • Conservatives in the Council Chamber men who had been prepared to a larger degree than othera to do what'

thav'could to further the best interests of the town. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. &mom Plaaroner responded on behalf of Sir Gilbert Greene% and said he knew why he had been asked to do so, namely, that he was one of Sir Gilbert's political lieutenants •he was not the rose, bur, politi- cally speaking, he 11,;,d Hied very near the rose. (Hear, hear.) He was sure Sir Gilbert would have been delighted to have been present that evening i 0 listen to the kind observations which had been made by Alder- man Burgess, and also to have seen the hearty manner in which the toast of his health as member for the borough was received. Everyone knew that Alderman tturgess was a strong political opponent of Sir Gilbert Greenall, but that did not prevent him showing respect to the member for Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. WHaaam OWEN presented the toast of the "Cor- poration." He could assure his hearers that the unpaid services of the Corporation of Warrington were not repaid with ingratitude, and as a very humble rate- payer, and he was not only speaking for himself, he had the presumption to speak for much larger ratepayers— (hear, hear)—he said that their services were repaid with a large amount of gratitude. (Applause.) He who came personally, in an official capacity, into contact with the Corporation, knew how arduous those duties were, _and how continually and well they were per- formed. (Applause.) Though the 'rates were spoken of in the country generally as being high, they knew that the Corporation were fighting against them, and would. ' get them as soon as possible down to a right proportion. To show how well the duties were carried on he would , like to call their attention to the name of Alderman Holmes, who, he believed, was the" father of the &un- , cil." (Applause.) He knew as a fact that, Alderman Holmes joined the Council when he (the speaker) was a baby—and they fpund him in harness still. (Applause.) Thataivas only one sample; he could point to other ' aldermen who, having passed the chair' had not retired on their laurels, but were still found doing their very best for the interests of the town. (Applause.) The MaYou said that at the last moment before coming there he received a letter from Councillor John Platt, in which he was sorry to say the writer excused himself I from attending on the ground that he was not very well. Under the circumstances, therefore, he thought they might substitute Alderman Chandley' name on the toast ' list for that ai Councillor Platt. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HOLMES was the first to respond to the toast, with which his own, Alderman Davies's, and Councillor Platt's names had been associated. He said it was extremely gratifying to the members of the Cor- poration to find that on a festal occasion like that their labours were recognized in such a manner. It was a high and honourable position to be a member of that Corpora- tion. He believed, and could say conscientiously, that the members of the Corporation at all imes endeavoured to discharge their duties to the ratepayers faithfully and well. (Hear, bear.) He had, it was true, been a mem- ber of that Corporation long time. Mr. Owen bad been good enough to describe him as the " father " of the Corporation—(hear, hear)—which meant that he had held a seat in the Council for a longer period than any otter gentleman; but he had before him his friend Alderman Webster, who. was a member of that Corpora- tion at its foundation.. (Applause,) He believed the ratepayers generally believed that the Corporation did their work as economically as possible, but whilst they did it economically they must endeavour to do it well— (hear, hear)—and they could not have work of that sort done without haying to pay for it. (Hear, hear) He had no doubt whatever that the future generations in Waningtort would reap the fruits of the work of the ' present Corporation, and think that they had had a good I • Corporation before them. (Applause. 1, 11, Alderman DAVIES remarked that it was a matter of congratulation and satisfaction that members of the Cora poration, at that late stage, of the evening, could all stand up and respond to they toast which had been so heartily given. (Laughtet.). He must say that in the department over which he (thespeaken), presided, which was the paving and sewerage of. the borough, he thought that his Committee stood above any other. .(Loud laughtel.) As regarded the future, he was going to suggest, though perhaps it was, a matter purely of busi- ness, that the members of each Committee should be entirely changed ; that all Committees should be recon- stituted •, that they should have an entire revolution to see whether they could do any better,. (Bear, hear, ansytengliter.) Alderman CIIANDLES urged the younger, members of the community of the borough to, imitate the example of their seniors by coming forward more willingly to serve their native town in the municipal department, in which they might shine if they so chose. (Hear, hear.) He thought that as a Corporation, they all very much 'regretted the fact that able men.= being. inwited to assist in, the conduct of the affaiss of their native town with one consent began to make excuse. (Hearahear.) Councillor F. A. Rosettes, ha proposing." The Borough. Magistrates," said they weze a body of gentlemen io whom, the burgesses at large owed a deep debt of grati- tude. (Hear, hear.) They wereall gentlemen who were highly respected and who received no effiolument for the duties which they performed, and he was glad of an 'opportunity of thanking them.f or the efficient manner in which they carried out those duties, so necessary to , the welfare andrgood conduct of the town. (Applause.) They were proud of the efficiency of the police„, and on oecasions that efficiency was remarked upon ha flattering ' terms, nat only outside, but within that Council chamber, ' in referring to the minutes of the Watch Committee.. It was a remarkable fact that when the minutes of that Committee were passed monthafter rieenth by the Council so little complaint was made ,• that, he thought, must be I dusato the 'astuteness of the borough magistrates-.. (gear, hen.) They exercised much firmness and eiscretion in dealing -with the offenders who were brought before I thews, Many of the members a the Bench attended to their magisterial duties at great personal ieconvanience, aad, so saved the borough the expense of having a saipendiary magistrate, for which every ratepayer ought to be thankful to them. (Hear, hear and applause.) Alderman WEBSTER responded. The magistrates„ he said, acted with the strictest impartiality in administer, hag, the law; they tempered justice with mercy, and bare in mind that " mercy is twice blest, it blesseth him that gives and him that takes," and when they had to pas sentence they , bore in mind the frailities of human nature, and strove to apportion the punishment to the backs of those who had to bear it. (Applause.), ALDERMAN Heasusore proposed "Success to the town and, rade of Warrington." With regard to the town itself he could not, as Mrs. Malaprop would say, go into " exotics " over ' its picturesque appearance,, nor into ecstateies, as, a higher grammatical authority than she would put it; nor could he paint it, as Claude Melnotte did his native place to the beautiftd Pauline, and say that “.• the air (of Warrington) is 'heavy with the slates and perfumes of orange groves, and marmers of.low lotus. tains, that gush fotth in the midst of roses "--(laughter) —for if he did there would be sure to spring up some unsympathetic patriot who, Would flatly contradict him aid say that the air WAS heavy with carboretted 14dr0gen, or tomething of the kind, and the stimulating aroma of" dear old Longford" and its tributary enter- cep ing depts. (Laughter.) Well, and if it was, they ought to be grateful and appreciative, for they had it on the unquestionable authority of their great sanitary Jupiter, Mr. Alderman Burgess—(iaughter and applause) —that Warrington could beast as low, if not a lower, death-rate than any manufacturing town in England of similar size. (Hear, hem) Then they hachtheir well ' paved, well-lighted streets; their inexhaustive supply of pure water. (Hear, hear.) ,Their educational establish- ments; their Musetima Library, and School of Art; their churches and chapels; their Infirmary with its tributaries for the allcseation of human sufferme—all of • which combined to indicate how worthy Warrington Was to be remembered in their toast lists on joyful occasions of that kind. (Applause.) Then, as to -the trade of the town. He was afraid it might be a great deal better than it was, although he was informed that they were as well off as most towns intheir wholesale and manufacturing .departments; but as 'regarded their domestie town trade, it was nothing like sotgood as it ought to., be,, and they all of thera could make it much better if, when they had money to spend foralornestic purposes, they spent it with their own shopkeepers, instead of running of to London, Liverpool, Manchester, and other places, thus depriving these who helped to, pay the rates, and bear the burthens, of that stimulating metallic circulating medium so necessary to give tone and vigour to their material and metaphorical constitutions. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. Jona Famatotron expressed the opinion that War- rington was very favourably placed for trade. (Hear, hear.) It had coal close at hand; it had railways com- peting for traffic ; and it had water carriage—a free river; and it would, he considered, be still more favour- ably situated, when that great undertaking the Ship Canal was finished. (Hear, hear.) He also considered that they had a Corporation second to none in Lanca- shire. (Laughter and applause.) They had, moreoirer, a Chamber of Commerce, which had protected and would continue to protect the trade of the town'. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Twoasas MomuslOaid that so far as the present state of trada was concerned, he did not suppose that there ever was such a volume of, orders on the books of ironmakers since he had known., Warrington. (Applause.) He did-not mean to say that those orders brought the enormous intere,st which had been received in times past,. but the town had to be thantful that workingmen were fully employed and received a fair day's wage for a fair day's vsork. (Hear, hear.) The tannirtg trade was also, he believed, in a flourishing condition. He wished the tanners all success and prospprity, and might their tribe never go down. (Laughter, and a Voice: "Nothing like leather.") He thanked the Corporation for the way they had managed the affairs of the town. (Hear, hear.) Councillor It. W. Fa.sarcomn gave the health of the &rough Surveyor. Use. Mr. T. LONODIN, in responding, s id that so far as ha ;own services were concerned, he had only tried to dllf what was right and to do everything well. (Applause.) He might possibly have recommended things to be done in the borough which were expensive, but he wished them to last, and he knew that if done properly they would turn out well. He rhight have had them aone in a " jerry " kied of way, but then they would not have lasted. As regarded the intercepting depots and Long- ford, he would leave that because he knew it was se to come out right, (Hear. hear.) There was nothingln it but What must turn out right, because they knew what the basis was—(laughter)—and he was certain it would come out right in the end. (Applause.) This concluded the toast list, and the:company separated, ,

div.head: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
div.p: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
BY MRS. J. K. SPENDER, Author of "Mr. Nobody," "Parted Lives," "Both in the Wrong," "Recollections of a Country Doctor," "Trust Me," &c.
CHAPTER XV. !. DR. HAVARD SPRAKSIVTJT.

"Don't be frightened," said Mrs. Wilson, in one of those appalling tones which always increase a fright tenfold, "your brother has met with an acci- dent. Sir Thomas has already sent for a doctor, and had his poor head bandaged up." _ _ _

_ Them, were bringing Raylinon- d in, who had been founehy his good old friend, Sir Thomas, as the latter was riding slowly back by the same road. He had put the lad on his own beast like the good Samaritan, attended carefully at a neighbouring inn to his wounds and bruises, and brought him home before the evenivg passed, with the hope of calming his sister's alarm. Raymond was not seriously hurt, and though he passed the corner of the lane which led to the manor-house with very different thoughts from those with which he had passed it that morning, the old baronet could not guess at the extent of the shock to the lad's nervous system. It was more for his own son's sake than the boy's • that Sir Thomas had taken to patronizing Raymond. He hated the lad's tendency to talk much about himself, hated his foreign ways, and was more inclined to blame than pity him for not protect- ing himself in this encounter. Why, Hubert would have been a match for any couple of such hounds—he'd have sent them spinning like ninepins," said Sir Thomas forgetting that his son had been trained in an English public school, and had had lessons from himself in the,pug-ilistic art. "The rogues couldn't have been much of it," Sir Thomas reasoned, "else they wouldn't have made off like a couple of rabbits directly they heard the thud of my horse's hoofs." The old man could not forgive the bodily weakness which made it impossible for Raymond to defend himself against ruffians. "There's a lot of contemptibleweakness abouthim3 without force enough to he downright " wieked, grumbled the old sportsman, ending, as usual, in pessimistic laments about the degeneracy of the villagers, the violent Radicalism of the newspapers, and what a mistake it was not. to hang a whole lot of these fellows.

"We shall never make a man of Ray," the doctor acknowledged despondently to his sister the next morning. "The French system of bringing up boys without cricket and football, boating or swimming, is irremediable. He will never take properly even to hunting or shooting. I should like to make a huge bonfire of all his paintings, poems, and novels—l should like to turn him out tohavesomegood, honest, stand-up fights in one et our English public schools." Margaret Havard smiled. Her brother was not-in so good a temper as usual,havingbeen summoned toßay- mond Catnpiori during the night. He had gone te see him with apparent alacrity, making a rule of never disobeying a summons of that kind. But he was too old not to miss his sleep during the small hours of the morning. And the sight of Ray's bedroom had die- pleased-him. There wore a number of photographs of actresses and singers—all, as Ursula declared, inno- cent enough—stuck singers—all; a large mirror which sr young man could hardly have needed. Whether intentionally or not, the doctor in his brusque movements knocked over an easel on which stood the portrait of a girl, half finished,with features he recognised. The •canvasfell face downwards, and, as the paint was still wet, a vague impression of the girl's features came off on the carpet. It was noticed that Dr. Havard only said " Humph !" with' a &nee of satisfaction, as he saw that he had injured both carpet and painting; and crossed the room to where Raymond lay white and shivering beneath an-eider- down counterpane drawn closelyoverhislimbs,though the weather was hot:

"Quite a commonplace ithing—a: mere ducking br the water. / thought nothing of it when I was a youngster, growled the doctor as he ordered awindow to be opened wider; and the eiderdown to be immedi- ately taken off. "You are angry wittimefor calling you up--andl ' don't wonder," said Ursula ;'" but I was anxious, "Oh, we shall make him all the better fey this, slight attack of illness before we have done with him," answered the doctor more gently—mollified in spite of himself by thoseappealing eyes of the colour of blue hyacinths, and., features delicately chiselled which reminded him of the suffering woman to, whom he had given a promise. "He has no right, to, be so like a woman, him- self," he grumbled the • next moment. And then aloud, turning to Ursula, " It is you who ought to. be sick! Nervous shocks of this sort shouitl, be, reserved for the •privilegulsex The doctor seemed to, the girl to be in! spirits at the prospect of keeping her brother under his own thumb for some time longer, "No one thinks of blaming, you," he said to the. 'sitter, who was not aware that she had been guilty of any imprudence—you, can't expect to put, grey heads on green shoulder."' "Thank you, my shoulders are white," reioiae& Ursula, with a mock courtesy. "The sooner ho leaves.tlais place the better. He'll go. on haying his own way—seems to me he alWays does:" 'growled the doctor; "but people are not always the better for havilig it." "To makes all sorts,of good resolutions." . _ .

"It is one thing to be, fertile in goord7iesolutions and quite another to, carry the out—a matter of m energy and will." Ursula tried to change the subject. She hatt never given hp hope of trying, to rehabilitate her brother in Dr. Havard's esteem, Hope was already re-asserting itself in her elastic nature. And when the mod man added, "He can't go on being a sort of Lar—as permanent household god for you all his life," she thought him a little hard. She had begun to 'reason with herself that it Wa..9 neither philosophic nor philanthropic of him, to form so severe a view of Raymond's character.. The two were nearer-qttarrel- ling than they had ever been before. But when .her kiwi; old friend said to herthe next day, after his conversation with Margaret, "Come, , I have 'a brilliant thought, a sudden insplration, about , your brother," she was willing enough to listen. ' She felt herself strenuously bound to oppose: anything which might seem. mikind to Raymond, but was ready enough to change her plans, or: even her opinions on sinr,ll matters, if, by so doing, she could give others pleasure: The plan was a• possible one. And if Raymond was not as the doeter said, "tremendously keen on it," and did not listen to it with unmitigated plea- sure, he had, at any rate, the grace not to oppose it obstinately. , The doctor, did not say to Ursula as ha had said to Margaret, that, the life which Ray was leading at St. Agatha's was a womanish, effeminate one, and that he ought to go put and be braced by meeting with his. fellows. But he put it in another way. All yonng Englishmen he' said, even country squires, were the better for academic training. Raymond was clever, and had read a little Latin and Greek already (the French system of training -being so unfortunately confined to that monotonous reading, of books) ; in fact, Ray was in , some re- spects—on the intellectual side, for instance, full of, promise ; it would.be a thousand shames not to allow him. the opportunity of making congenial friendships; and, in fine, a University education, though it had its risks, had also tempting possibili- ties,and might be the great hope of salvation for him. Ursula listened, in sublime ignorance of the laborious preparation which would be required, and wonderino, why .th'e doctor had never made the sug- gestion before. She did not guess that he only sug- gested it now because he was at his. wit's end as to: what to do with Ray. Her vivid imagination had already flown onwards and was picturing to her what the dohs and other area would say to a young man as French in his ways as Ray. "Pa' si bete I" said the latter when the plan Isms first proposed to him. He objected to putting . his head into a noose and subjecting himself to be held in red-tapism by deans and proctors. But since Ursula had held the purse-strings more tightly, she was not so popular with her brother. ",There is too much brilliancy about/ her. I like soniAtimes to be without her—it's a Bert of rest," he went so far as to acknowledge to himself. "We can't be Siamese twins always," he ex- plained to her, with a new sort of nonchalance. He was beginning already to weary of St. Agatha's. And Ursula, as we know, had wearied of it long before. "1 vilsh they would be 'good enough to start a ghost—at least it would give us something to . talk about," she acknowledged as the days passed on. ' The idea gained upon her of planning for Raymond to travel with a tutor, and commence his preparation for "Smalls." [Jr. Havard had found a friend who ' could undertake the post of " coach" during the next ' six months. But meanwhile what was to become of : Ursula? Her capricious whims as Sir Thomas some- what sourlysuggested, might do much' mischief to the people of St. .Agatha's . It was a problem which took a little time to solve. And then she decided to go to London. • • • (To be continued.)

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

THE GERMAN EMPEROR'S TOUR.— THE POPE IN INTERVIEW. Roars, SUNDAY NIOHT.—The Pope is not at all satis- fied with the interview he had with the Emperor. °wing to the extreme brevity of the visit, he had not time to express what be wished to say. The Pope is always rather diffuse in speaking, and does not go atraight to the point. His Holiness began the conversa- tion by speaking of the la.St visit he had received from the late Emperor Frederick, when the latter was still Crown Prince. Before he had time to broach the subject of the Roman question, Prince Henry LA Prussia was announced. It seems that the EfllPeror had purposely given his brother orders to °°lne before the time, so as to curtail the CCM- versation, which might have been difficult to keep 1.1 I). the Emperor not wishing to vex his Catholic sub- lects, and at the same timeronsidering the Roman trees- lion completely an internal Italian problem. It is a fact that Prince Henry arrived 20 minutes sooner than he \vas expected. The toasts at the Court dinner have given great offence at the Vatican. Tney felt qtaite cer- tain there that the Emperor . would not speak of the Unity of Italy; therefore the toast in which he not only °Poke of the united country, but of Rome its capital, took the Vatican quite by surprise. The Pontiff has Se n expressed his displeasure to some of 'his Court. The general impression at the Vatican may be summed OP as follows. The Emperor has given the. Pope the outward show of satisfaction, but not the substance. OPENING OF THE FRENCH CHAMBERS. The French Chambers were re-opened 'yesterday, and the debate on the Budget was fixed for the 22nd, in "tolia/ice with the wish of M. Floquet. Subsequently The Premier submitted a bill for the revision of the Con- Stitution. M. Floquet, in introducing the Revision Bill. expressed his belief that it was calledlor by the legiti- tnate wishes of the country. The Government, he,con- tinued, considerei that the powers of the National As- sembly must not be curtailed, nor must a programme be prescribed for it; but the Chambers could come to an understanding as to the measure of revisionto be recommended. It was ultimately decided to refer the bill to the existing Committee, motions to refer it to a SPecial Committee and for urgency being rejected. , kmnsiclerable irritation Was CAUSPCI outside the Chamber by the posting of placards bearing the words:" Down with the Robbers." The placards were removed by the Dolice. The Temps says they were posted by order of a Boulangist journal.

A GLOOMY OUTLOOK IN EGYPT. Owing to the rapid fall of the Nile. the 'loss to the country will be fully £300,000. Cotton .prospects still continue good, and a satisfactory yield may reasonably be expected. The financial outlook is at present some- 'what gloomy. It is. nevertheless, hoped that mattere rnay yet turn out better than indicated by present ap- pearances. Private advices 'from Spakimr describe the situation there as becoming serious, and the authoritirs • are now awakening to the fact that something must. he done without delay, either in the direction of a large In- crease of the military establishment. Or else by. the evacuation of the posts at present held at Suakint.:and Wady Haifa.

IRELAND.
A force of police accompanied the sub-sheriff from Westport, on Monday, to evict a number of families or. the Gibbon estate.

Cardinal Moran has subscribed £5O to the Parnell indemnity fund, which has now reached nearly £B,OOO. The cardinal says he adds his mite, to enable the Irish Parliamentary party to defend itself against the vile aspersions which the enemies of Ireland have sought ts cast noon it.

In Dublin. on Monday, Judge Boyd issued an order of attachment against Mr. Pierce Mahony, M.P., for inciting tenants on the Delmege Estate, Co. Limerick, not to re- ceive an abatement of 30 per cent. made by the Court from the receiver to offer them. The plan of campaign is adopted on the estate, the tenants asking 57i per cent. reduction.

Father MC...Fadden of Gweedore, was released from Deny Prison, on Tuesday, two days before the expira- tion of !Ms sentence. His friends had become aware of prospective release, and a considerable crowd gatheree. The rev, gentleman made a speech, saying he was betttr than when he went in.

A serious not took place -on Saturday night. crEeited lw some persons who were Teturnine from Swanligbar fait. In the row a man named M'Crovern was stabbed in several places in a terrible manner by a man mined Thomas Doran. The injhred man died on Monday, and tie assailant and another man have been arrested.

The Marquis of Londonderry. Lord Lieutenant of Ire- land. Lady Londonderry, and suite visited Belfast on Saturday, Woven a new free library. The town was de- corated for the occasitm, and the Streets wete"thronged with people. The Mayor received their Excellencies at the Library, which was declastsd open amid much cheering.

There were several evictions on Saturecy on the Leahy estate, and Mr. .Toha Roche, of Woodford, was again arrested because of his refusal to pay the fine imposed by the resident magistrate for trespass on cer- tain lands. This is the fourth time in a-year that Mr. Roche has been arrested under the CoerciOn Act: but he did not go to prinon, his friends, owing tothe state of his neattil, paying the fine withertn his knowledge.

Lord 'Londonderry, apeaking at a luncheon given by the Mayor of Belfast on Saturday, said the trade of Ire- land vies steadily reviving, and prosperity, peace, and happiness were returning to the law-abiding population of some parts of the corn:try. fie quoted returns to show that in a year Patel' the passinref the Chimes-Set there was a decrease oT 28 per cent in serious agrarian ontrages, arid he was glad to add tbat intimidation was steadily diminishing, and the number of persons boy- cotted hadfalso decreased.

div.head: MR. MORLEY'S REJOINDER TO MR. BALFOUR..
div.p: MR. MORLEY'S REJOINDER TO MR. BALFOUR..

- - Mr. John Morley writes to a correspondent that Mr. Balfour, in the recent controversy, carefully avoids a plain answer to a plain question. Be will not say that Mr. Chamberlain was right in asserting that every prisoner under the Crimes • Act had broken the law in the way in which be was said to have broken it, and he Will not say that Mr. Morley was wrong in directly con- tradicting that proposition. Mr. Morley again quotes from f.x,s.nsarcl" Mr. Balfour's promise that in every case under the Crimes Act the right of appeal shall be given, and maintains that the promise has not been kept. Mr. Morley admitted that he was led erroneously to suppose that the sentence imposed by the Coercion Court in a particular case had not been reversed on ap- peal. Mr. Balfour was perfectly free to dwell upon this inaccuracy, with whatever strength of language he might choose. The error did not touch the argument, still less did it place the Coercion Court in a worse posi- tion than that in which it had placed itself. Mr. Hal- four's second letter, like the first, is a piece of pure mystification.

The work consists of three parts, under the heads of Histori- cal. 'Controversial, and Statistical. The latter, dealing with the results of similar cases in which operations have been performed, is, of course, more directly inter- esting to the medical profession. The historical part forma the major portion of the volume, and in it is re- lated in chronological order the story of the Emperor's ill- nese,with many incidental reflections on the professional and personal action of the German doctors. ' THE LONDON MURDERS. The Home Secretary has sent the folloWing repiyte Mr. Rusk, of Alderney-road, Mile End, in answer to a re. quest that a free pardon might be offered to the accotn. plice or accomplices of the Whitechapel murderer : " October 12. Sir,—l am directed by the Scretaty of State to thank you for the suggestions in your letter of the 7th inst on the subject of the recent Whitechapel murders, and to say, in reply, that from the first the Secretary of State has had under consideration the ques- tion of granting a pardon to accomplices. It is obvious that not only must such a grant be limited to persons who have not been concerned in contriving Grin actually committing the murders, bnt the expediency and pro- priety of making the offer must largely depend on the nature of the information received from day to day, which is being carefully watehed with a view to deter- mining that question. With regard to the offer of a reward, Mr. Matthews has, under the existing circum- stances, nothing to add to his former letter." The murder scare has spread to other parts of the metropolis, as an instance of whit,h, about noon on Saturday, a sensation was occasioned in the locality of High Holborn. A gentleman was proceeding along Holborn, in the direction of the City, when he was sud- denly pounced upon by a strange man of the labouring class, who exdaimed ia an excited manner, " This is Jack the Ripper:' A-struggle ensued, and the two fell heavily to the ground. The scene soon attracted a very large crowd of peoPle, who quickly collected, thinking that the Whitechapel murderer had been arrested. Much excitement prevailed, and the man was conveyed to the police station. Such incidents are traceable to the effect of the threatening letters which have been circu- lated purporting to haVe Leen written by *Jack the Ripper."

div.head: IWEDDING TRIP IN ,A BALLOON.
div.p: A IWEDDING TRIP IN ,A BALLOON.

• kdecpatch from Providence, Rhode Island, says the greatest novelty at the Rhode Inland State Pair at Narragansett Park was the rcarriage. of a young Pro- vidence couple in the balloon Commonwealth. They were: Edward J. DOM'S :and his • intended, Miss Mar- garet • ituckley. Davis is a shipping clerk, and for a long time be ,has • been engaged to Miss •Burirley. They mitred over the -rnatter of the publio .rrierriage and a kballoon ascension at • leisure. and made,2ll preparations for the event. MI day long the big Commonwealth swayechin a lively wind, bumped against the ground, and drove ,the immense multitude 'back. About everyone am the ground expressed their fears that the couple would finally back out. The crowd had. been gathering sell day, and at feur o'clock. the time set for the marriage and ascension, there were 30,000 .people.present. An benr later, when the Rev. E. D. Hall, of ,St. Paul's' Methodist Episcopal Church, came .upon) the scene. followed by the bridal couple, there were 0,0111:1 more. There was intense excite- ment as the your,z moot., stood before the clergyman. who proceeded to make them man and wife after the usual form. The bride bore herself with becoming modesty, and blushed when the groom kissed her.. She was dressed in. white satin, and her face beamed with eagerness for her ,Domantic wedding trip. Profeesor James K. Allen. the tororiaut, entered the car, and the lines were zest off amid great excitement. The balloon rose rapidly, and the great erdwd cheered lustily. The bride responded by waving her handkerchief, and the groom waved his hat. The balloon sailed off far to the north-east and was soon lost in the darkness. The couple, it is understood, made the aecension for a money consideration. The balloon landed in a cedar swamp near North Easton, Ma.ssachusetts, in the evening. The balloon dragged two mites across the swamp, and the young couple had to cling to the ropes to escape drown- ing. They were finally rescued, and made the rest of their 'wedding journey by rail.

It has been generally supposed that the discovery of the fate of Sir John Franklin, es ascertained by the members of the expedition under Sir Leopold Mc.Clin- took. and published by Murray, in the Journal of the Fox, had tor ever set the subject at rest. But we are in a position to state that Mr. T. Fisher rinwin has secured for publication a new work which will explain in a marvellous manner the real cause that led to the dis- covery, and which was only known to Lady Franklin and a few of her most intimate friends. The facts, which are now for the first time to be made public, will, in their sensational disclosures, rank amongst the literary events of the season.

div.head: GENERAL E
div.p: GENERAL E
Peter Anderson, quarry worker, Aberdeen, was charged on Monday with the murder of his wife, who, it is alleged, he stabbed in a quarrel. He was remanded. - -

_ Mr. T. Walker, stationmaster at Wakely, on the North British Railway, was run over ana killed on Saturday. He was 69 years of age, and had been 30 years in the company's service. FATAL FIRE IN LONIDON.—A fire broke out in a dwelling an.! workshop near Berner-street, Whitechapel, on Satur- day, and the flames spread with such rapidity that exit by the staircase was impossible, and three women, lean- ing from the upper windows, were injured. One of them, Mrs. Suboifski, died later at the London Hospital.

ATTACKED EY A BEAR.—At Franklin's Gardens, Northampton...on Saturday, John Gotch, a former at- tendant, ventured into the bear pit, and was savagely attacked by one of the animals. Several volunteers hurled their 'bayonets at the bear, and succeeded in rescuing the man, but not until the flesh had been torn from his At an iflquest held at Oldbury, respecting the death of an ironworker's child named Dunwoody. it was stated ' 'hat the father turned the mother and child out on Mon- day night. The child died, and the father refused to allow the corpse to be brought to the house, and told the mother to take it to the mortuary. The father was severely censured by the coroner. Frederick Bass, gilder, has been charged at Stratford with attempting to poison his wife and three •childred by putting a quantity of oxalic acid into some tea which had been prepared for the family meal. He immediately gave himself up to the police, and confessed what he had done. His wife, finding the tea had a peculiar taste, did not partake of it. nor did her children. Prisoner was remanded, that he might be examined by the doctors as to his state of mind.

His left leg had to 'be .amputated, and the right cue was still •useless. The jury awarded £4,500 damages. !Tsar. or NINE HUNDRED Farc.—A shocking colliery occident is reported from Merthyr Tydvil. A workman 'named Hughes was engaged effecting 'repairs in the • shaft of the Merthyr Valley Colliery, when be missed his footing, and was precipitated headlong into the pit, fall- ,lag a depth of aine hundred feet. The body was ter- ribly mutilated when recovered. A miner named Stephen Williams, employed at he Mountain Level Col- iiiery, was also killed by is fall of voof whilt working at 'the coal face with his companion. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO SIR WILMIAM CIINLIFFE BROOKS, M.P.—Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, M.P., returning home in the moonlight, after deer-stalking in the Forest of i-Glen Tana, Scotland, on Saturday, fell,at an awkward place, breaking both bones of his left arm._ The honour- able baronet is progressing favourably, and hopes to be in his place in Parliament on the opening day of the autumn session. It will be remembered that Sir William broke the same arm some months ago by a fall as he was proceeding to the House of Commons.

SHOCKING CHARGE AGAINST A MOITIER.—OR Saturday, a young woman named Heason was brought up at Sutton Petty Sessions, charged with attempting to murder her two young children by starving them to death. The accused had been for some time given to 'habits of intemperance, and when supplied with bread. and Anglo-Swiss condensed milk wby the relieving officer for the support of her children she sold the nourishment to other neighbours to get drink. Her two children when discovered were in a shocking state, being fear- fully emaciated and covered witlyvermin. Prisoner was • remanded.

He has.bequeathed everything over which he had testamental", power to the Queen's Maids of Honour! The furniture, pictures, and bric-a- brac of Knole House which Are not .beirlooms are to be put-Up to auction for the benefit of the young ladies in question, and are expected to fetch R50;000 alone. Lori Sackville, as is well known, was engaged for many years in litigation with his elder brother, .the Earl of De Is Warr, the subject in dispute .being Knole House and the ostates kettle(' with it. These now pass ‘tio Her Majesty's Minister at Washington, and the income is not less than Eickpoo a year. But the ill-feelings engendered by the protracted litigation with the elder brother appear to have been extended by Lord Sackville -to his family generally, hence the extraordinary good 'fortune of the Queens Maids of Honour.

Tun WAGES QUESTION TN TEE COAL TRADR.—Mr. r Ashton. secretary of the Lancashire Miners 'Federation, has:reocived a letter from the secretary of the Oldham and Ashton Coal Owner's Association, which covers the creater,part of Cheshire as well as Lancashire. asking that arrangements should be made for a conference of the miners' representatives and the Employers' Associa- tion on the Question of the advance of 10 per cent. A conference will be held. it is understood, oo the 22nd inst., in Manchester. It is hoped that an amicable Arrangement will then be made 4 The other districts nci doubt fall in with the arrangement .cenie to at the conference. The North Wales colliers on Saturday ,gave notiae to the masters for an advance in wages of ten per cent, as advised by the Manchester Conference. The South Staffordshire miners came out on strike. on Monday. under notices for a 10 per cent. advance. A mass meeting of Miners was held at Oldhill, Stafford- stare, on Monday. to consider the wages question. It. was decided that the miners should resume work at 5 per cent, increase until the 27th inst.., when a demand will he made for an additional 5 per cent., a strike to follow if not conceded.

div.head: FATALITY AT A WARRINGTON IRON WORKS.
div.p: FATALITY AT A WARRINGTON IRON WORKS.

Mr. 13. Brighouse, coroner for south-west Lanca- shire, held an inquiry at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey Bridges, on Wednesday, touching the death of Samuel Platt, aged 16, who lived with his parents in Liverpool-road..--Peter Platt, father of the de- ceased, who appeared to be much affected. said that he was an engine-driver, employed at the works of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., Sankey Bridges. Witness, deceased, and another son of witness all worked toge- ther, the deceased in the capacity of pointsman, and his brother as "shunter." About half-past seven o'clock on Wednesday morning, the 3rd inst., he and his sons were engaged in distributing wagons through the works. He was about :to collect four wagons, which were in a siding. He siw the deceased turn the number one point, and, not noticing that he had left it, he moved the engine on and closed the wagons up. As he did so, he heard a shout from the deceased, and looking back, saw that he was caught between the buffers. He reversed the engine, and, going to the back of the wagons, he saw the deceased in his brother's arms. They took the lad home and he was attended,by Dr. Joseph, but on Sunday morning he expired.—Arthur Platt, brother of the deceased, corroborated the statement of his father. Asked how, in his opinion the accident I happened, he said he thought the deceased must have been standing on the brake, when the wagons were "bumped.," and that the recoil threw him between the buffers.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," joining with the Coroner in expressing their sympathy with the father.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COITNCIL. LOCAL 'ELECTORAL DIVISIONS.

The areas of the new electoral divisions in the county of Cbester were finally determined on Monday, at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, held in the Courthouse, Knutsford. Appended is a list of the townships constituting the local divisions and the estimated population of each place : . _

APPLETON Divlstox.—To consist of the following townships in the Runcorn Union Rural Sanitary District, viz. :—Antrobus. 430; Appleton-with-Hull, 2,067;. Crowley, 196 ; Great Budworth, 532; Hatton, 365 ; Seven Oaks. 183; Stretton. 396; Walton Inferior, 498; Walton Superior, 246 ; Whitley Inferior, 214; Whitley Superior,. 306. And the following townships, forming the part of the Warrington Union Rural Sanitary District in this county, viz.: Grappenhall, 788; Latchford (part out- side municipal borough of Warrington), 323 ; 498. Total, 7,040. _ _ _

LYMM Dtioios.—To consist of the following town- ships, viz. :—Lymm Local Board District: Lymm, 4,665. Altrincham Union Rural Sanitary District: Agden, 104; Ashley, 385 ; Bollington, 272 ; High Legh, 850 ; Milling- ton, 266 ; Partington, 438; Rostherne, 382; Warburton, 426. Twat, 7,788.

RUNCORN NORTH DITISION.—To consist of part of the district of the Buncorn Improvement Commissioners, viz. :—Runcorn: That portion lying northward and north-east of the following boundary, that is to say— From the Weston township boundary along the northern side of the Runcorn and Weston Can through Francis Dock to Swing Bridge Wharf, thence along the northern side of the new Tine of locks to Waterloo Bridge, thence along the. northern side of the Bridgewater Canal to where Big Pool enters the canal, thence across the canal to the Big Pool, and thence along the eastern side of the Big Pool to the boundary of the township of Halton. .Note.—A separate register of electors can be made out for the above division. _

Rmicons Sou = Divtsiox.—To consist of the remain- ing part of the district of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, viz. :—Runcorn: That portion lying southward of the boundary defining Runcorn North Electo4al division. The population of the whole district is 15,126. Note.—A separate register of electors can be made out for the above division.

_ FRODSHAM Drvisms.—To consist of the following townships si uate in the Runcorn Union Rural Sanitary District, viz. : Alvanley, 321 ; Frodsham, 2,489 ; Frodsham Lordship, 1,087; Helsby, 812; Kingsley, 1,207 • Kingswood, 235; Manley, 306; Newton-by Frodsham, 119 •, Norley, 721. Total, 7,297. DARESBURY DIVISION.—To consist of the following townships, situate in the Runcorn Union Rural Sanitary District, viz. :—Acton Grange, 173; Aston-by-Sutton, with Middleton Grange, 285; Aston Grange, 33; Bartington, 98 ; Clifton, 203; Daresbury, 139 ;Dutton, 452 ; Halton, 1,125 ; Keirewick, 83: Moore, 398 ; Newton- by-Daresbury, 189; Nor on, 345; 580; Stockham, 25; Sutton, 377 ; Weston, 1,684. Total, 6,167.
