Sin MoitELL Mecxrarzies' work on "The Fatal Illness of Frederick the Noble" has certainly Proved as sensational as it was expected to be; ut the whole controversy exhibits the specialists 111., a most unfavourable light. If the English loctor is right in his conclusion, he has been einiost as" badly treated" by the German doctors se was the late Emperor himself. Sir MORELL lakes it out that the German physicans lie the suspicion of having produced" artificial eencer " by their bungling with the galvano- eentery. He thinks the application of the red-hot Wire to the throat eveuy day for a fortnight was a °. ery rude way of treating a delicate organ. But It is against Professor BERGMANN that the most 4eriQus charge is made. It is stated that in chang- "4 the tube on one occasion, he thrust it into the litteell instead of the windpipe, and produced such a orrible wound that under the circumstance it troved "the death warrant of the Emperor." ,ndeed, it is estimated that the royal sufferer would 'aye lived at least ten months longer if he had not been mal-treated in this unskilful fashion. On the I°.tlier hand,the Germans charge the English specia- lat with having failed to detect that the disease w''-11 cancer when the factivas patent to themselves; 4.4thd'that it was he who did irreparable injury to f e;t'nperor's throat by removing healthy instead "Iseesed tissue for the purpose of examination. nlead of removing part of the cancerous growth, 15 Said to have carried off a portion of the the throat.---In the- midst, of all may well exclaim with

~ poet Pope : • • , - _, "Who shall decide when doctors disagree I" lt is sad, it is pitiful, to think that the last days st the life of a truly noble man were darkened by the knowledge that the doctors who attended him were furiously jealous of each other, and that he Ilkl too much reason to believe that he had not l'oceived all the benefit that he ought to have re- e,eived from their combined skill and attention. The _figures which Sir MORELL MAC- kktris gives prove conclusively that, when . is established in the throat, the chances of recovery after operation for its removal 4e exceedingly small. The German comment 11Pon this is that it does not do to wait until the saocer has made progress; that it is the cut in , - that saves nine; and that if the operation sad been performed when they first detected sNicer the Emperor Frederick might have been stive to-day. Ile toid the audience that he was not illilarried, and we suspect that this muse be because Ile loves himself alone; but it was BALFOUR; At• Penn, BALFOUR from beginning to end. His 3%icism does not permit him to have faith .in 443 thing or anybody excepting Mr. BALFOUR. He li:l2afesses to treat the attacks that are made upon 21.0 as, in the language of the " MixAno," "a 711'ce of innocent meriimeat." "I do not," he 4" allude allude so much to the Irish abuse which 8 the Nationalist newspapers in Ireland. That matter of course; it has been a blessing I:llellsafed in 'equal measure to my predecessors myself." \ This is a plain statement, but is it b e Will anyone, Liberal or Tory—always lieepting Mr. BALFOTJR—say that Mr. JOHN he°,lllEY was abused "in equal measure" whilst he till:office as Irish Secretary P It is notorious tit was not so; it was recognised that Mr a h°llLirr was honest and sincere, and that he had 142, eart-felt desire to better the lot of the Irish *0844'4. He showed this by deeds as well as tdsf and the result is that, while the name of 41-roun is execrated, that of MORLEY is revered. ka: Irish Secretary further said ;--"Probably the it4tritY—l believe the m4ority—of those I 1,41788 do not belong to the political party of it has been all through my political life my to be a member." How eagerly the Tories
The

and the Liberal Unionists hug delusions as to the composition of their audiences •If the speaker is MP. JOSEPH CHAMBERLAIN, he assumes' that the people he addresses are for the most part Liberals —of the Unionist type—when, if he had his weather eye half open, he would see that his hearers are one-tenth Unionist and nine-tenths Tory. I And now Mr. BALFOUR is trying it on; he rises to address a lot of Tory squires, and proceeds to speak of them as if they were chiefly Liberals who had become as much enamoured of him as he is of himself. It is amusing rather than edifying to read the elaborate arguments Which the Irish Secretary brings forward to show that it is better, on the whole, that Liberal Unionists should not become part and parcel of the Tory party. The very fact, however, that such an issue is an open question is really the most damaging thing that can be said against these questionable Liberals. As the French proverb lias it, he who excuses accuses; it shows how little of the Liberal there is really left of them. But perhaps the most offen- sive part of Mr. BALFOUR'S speech is that in which he has the audacity to talk of " drawing closer the bonds of union which at present hold together the separate portions of the Empire." It is as if the hangman were to ask his victim to grow sent. mental ,over the rope which is to strangle him.' The Irish Secretary poses, as usual, as one of "the custodians of public morality of the country." Het always does that; it is the dog returning to hil vomit; but it would be something towards the improvement of his own morality if he would explain how he cape to break his word in the matter of appeals under the---Coercion AOC BALFOURISH is never other than disagreeable, but when it champions the cause of "public morality," it is more than disagreeable; it is nauseous.

"TOUCH AND GU."
The Salt Ring has given rise to proposals for a Coal Ring, an Iron Ring, and a Copper Ring. There is less said just now about that ring of rings—the wedding ring.

It is said that the Chancellor of the Exchequer will make it known when Parliament meets that he has decided to abandon the Van and Wheel Tax scheme. We predicted that it would be weal or woe Nvit'h the project: it is woe.

If the scheme for the amalgamation of Man- chester and Salford comes off, Manchester—for Salford will be absorbed—will have a population of 600,000, and will thus become the second city of the empire. "The Manchester man" will be proud then.

"It is stated that the heir to a baronetcy, who recently eloped with a London bar Maid, has been received with his bride in the bosom of his family." Baronetcy abd barmaid seem to run in couples. But what of the coat-of-arms? Does an alliance of this kind mean a " bar sinister ?"

Prince Bismarck's way of answering Sir Morell Mackenzie is to suppress his book. This is-very effectual—for a time. It is like trying to get rid of a cork by pushing it under water. The weak point of the plan is that the cork soon pops up again. It will be so with the book; it will re- appear amongst the Germans, despite Prince Bis- marck's coercion.

There was a tremendous rash for shares in the great Salt Syndicate; and, according to all accc unts, men of straw in some cases were apply- ing for shares as thcugh they were millionaires. It is needless to say that speculators of this class have been disappointed with the allotments. Many of those who calculated on a big catch have not so much as had a nibble. •

"Mr. Joseph Biggar, M.P., who has recently become a total abstainer,made his first appearance on the temperance platform in Dublin, on Monday night, when he addressed a meeting held in cele- bration of the anniversary of the birth of Father Mathew." The temperance movement is making headway; Sir William Harcourt's was a big con- version ; but Isft this a " bigger '? "

• "In opening the Michaelmas Sessions, at Lim- erick, on Tuesday, Mr. Purcell congratulated the grand jury ori the peaceable state of the city; this being the third maiden-session in Limerick this year.' It would be interesting to know how Mr. Chamberlain would reconcile this fact with his theory of Irish corruption. But perhaps it is Joseph's way now to stick to the theory, and be hanged to the fact ? "

There • seems to have been a wholesale and a systematic supply of liquor to the navvies at Elles- mere Port by unlicensed persons. But the police have been on their track, with the result that heavy fines have been imposed. It seems that, in order to make sure of a conviction, two constables obtained work as navvies and in this way they got at the illicit taps. The real navvies have, it seems, been entertaining angels unawares.

" Truth " says :—" I hear that the marriage of Prince Alexander of Battenberg and Princess Victoria of Prussia will probably take place within the next few weeks, in the private chapel at Windsor Castle—of course, without any State ceremony." These Battenbergs are wide awake; they don't, as Shakespeare has it, see fit to "batten on the moor"; they know better than that when they have "on this fair mountain leave to feed."

Referring to the "Times'" statement of case against Mr. Parnell, the " World " says :—" The authenticity of the letters will hardly be ques- tioned seriously, but the evidence of the letters would be hardly sufficient without more evidence of a stronger and more condemnatory nature,of which there is also plenty. There was some difficulty at first in making Mr. Parmßl realise that it was necessary he should, give his serious attention to the matter." Does anybody take the " World" seriously when it says "the authenticity of the letters would hardly be questioned P" The opinion of the 'real world is just the reverse of that of the paper " World."

• • Miss Anna Parnell is included in the " Times4 " list of persons who have been guilty of nobody knows what terrible things. We remember hear- ing her speak some years ago. She gave bne the impression of being ready to make great sacrifices for the freedom of her native land. She is sister, we presume, of the Irish leader, and of Miss Fanny Parnell, who wrote the touching poem, "After Death," in which occur the following beautiful lines : Au! the tramp of feet victorious! I should hear them, Mid the shamrocks and the mosses, And my heart should toss within the shroud and quiver As a captive dreamer tosses.

The French have got beyond Voltaire's flippant criticism of Shakespere. They displayed genuine admiration at the unveiling, on Sunday, of the statue to the world's poet. A contemporary'com- menting on the event says :—" It is not a little significant that one of the first of French- theatre managers to place Shakspere's plays before his audiences—Pierre de Laplace— rendered the title of a comedy called "Love's Last Shift," "La Derniere Chemise del' Amour." This is good, but there is a story told of a translator of Shakespere who, dealing with the well-known lines beginning —"Out, out! brief eandle!" rendered the phrase thus—" Get out, you short candle!" That was a "last shift."

On Wednesday, over 400 miners resumed work at the Ebenezer Pits, Tipton, Staffordshire, at the full advance of 10 per cent. INTEMPERANCE CURED.—A wealthy American Lady whose only son was fcr years a-s lave to intemperance, after seeking in vain for a cure, and trying all known remedies, at last found a simple means that cured and save him from a drun- kard's grave. Anyone suffering or desiring to help others in this worthy cause, by sending a self-addressed stamped en- velope to M. James Holland, 25, Hart-st., High Holborn, London, will receive this information free of charge. Men- thols this paper.-41.44.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY RI7NCORN.—At the weekly meeting of the members of this Society, on Friday evening, Captain Le Couteur delivered an interesting lecture on the descripti9n of the tropical regions. ST. JoHN's CIIURCH, WESTON.—The harvest festival was celebrated on Friday evening, when the Rev. J. W. Maitland preached an able sermon to a numerous audi- ence. On Sunday the Rev. J. H. Wileoekeon' of Weston Point, conducted the sermon and preached. The church was decorated in the usual lavish and attractive manner.

TEOSTRE ROYAL,RuNcoRN.—On Thursday evening Mr. O'Beirnes Opera Company commenced a three nights engagement in the Theatre Royal.with the performance of Wallace's Maritana." The caste was a very strong one, and the audience frequetxtly expressed their approval. Last night "Faust" was represented, and to-night the ever popular "Bohemian Girl" will fill the programme. • _ HOLY TRINITY CAI7RCII RUNCORN —The annual harvest . _

festival was commenced on Friday evening, when the Rev. Dr. Camm preached an appropriate sermon to a good congregation. On Sunday the pulpit was occupied by th‘Rev. Dr. Bartle, of Southport, who preached two stirring discourses ro crowded congregations. Specially selected music was effectively rendered by the choir, Mr. J. Hughes, deputy organist at Chester Cathedral, presid- ing at the organ. The sacred edifice was artistically decorated with the fruits and flowers of the earth..

Sr. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES.—The hkrvest thanks- giving services In connection with this church were continued on Sunday. The sacred edifice, as in former' years, was chastely decorated with fruit and flowers. In the morning, the Rev. W. Flaherty, vicar of Trinity Church, Parr Mount, St. Helens, preached; and in the evening the Rev 7. W. Davies, B.A. vicar of All Saints'. Churck, Liverpool, preached. The harvest anthem, "Fear not, 0 land (Caleb Simper), was rendered by the choir. Offertories were taken in aid of the organ and vestry fund. WIDNES FREE Prramc LIBRARY.—During the month lof September 4,595 books were borrowed from the library of this institution, being an increase of'2Bl on the corresponding month last 'year. The average daily issue was 184. The total 'attendance at the reading room during the month was 12,219, averaging 489 for each of the 25 days the Library had been open. The Local Government Board have declined to sanction the expenditure of £2O for the purpose of providing free lectures for the people, but arrangementsarenevertheless being made for the delivery of a course of popular lectures on scientific and literary subjects. WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY.—On Thursday evening a meeting was held in Simms Cross Board School,with the object of discussing the desirability of resuscitating the Widnes Choral Society, which was suspended two years ago in consequence of its indebtedness. Through the exertion of Mr. W. S. Callander (hon. sec.) and other officials the society is now free from debt, and hopes are entertained of again resuming the rehearsals and placing the society on a sound footing. After considerable dis- cussion the subject was adjourned to a future meeting. Mr. J. Morrison has consented to undertake the duties of conductor gratuituously on condition that an accompanist is secured and the society placed in good order. •

ELLESMERE-ST., RUNCORN, IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—The present session in connection with the above society has been commenczd under favourable circumstances. The following officers hariben -electetti—Presiclentrmin—fik- Minshull ; vice-president, Mi. J_ Stubbs ; secretary,-Mr. James Turnbull ; treasurer, Mr. T. Clarke. A paper was:read by the Rey. E. Hall, on Friday evening, on the subject of The recent discussion on the m•rriage ques- tion." Mr. Hall conteniled that ‘! marriage is not a failure," that a majority of the married people are more contented, more settled in their habits, more comfortable in their homes, and more useful to the community than those who remain single. Some causes of " failure were pointed out, the principal being the want of thorough knowledge of each other before marriage, the mercenary motives of many people, drunkenness, and the want of nlutual confidence bet‘men husband and wife. A discifssion followed, in which Messrs. Stubbs, F. J. Poole, and J. Scragg took part. . . .

STUBBS' iI7RNITITTIE CREAM.—For giving a brilliant gloss to all kinds of mahogany and French polished furniture with half the usual labour, use Stubbs' Furniture Cream. Sold in bottles, id., 2d., and 3d.—lsaac Stubbs, Lowlands-road. Run corn.-Advt.

BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY AT RUNCORN.— The annual meeting of the Runcorn Branch of this Society was held in Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday evening. There was only a moderate attendance. Mr. J. Meadowcroft occupied the chair' and was supported by the Rev. W. Preston M.A., H. Berson (Superintend- ent Wesleyan Minister) F Barnes M.A. (Congregational minister, Chester) and J. D. Thomas.—The Chairman, inhis opening address, said from what he knew of the operations of the Society, he thought it merited the sympathy of everyone, and the support of both minis- ters and laymen.—The Rev. H. Berson urged that the amount sent from Runcorn to the parent Society should be doubled.—The Rev. J. D. Thomas also advocated the claims of the Society, and then the Rev. F. Barnes (who attended as a deputation' delivered a speech in which he referred to the work of the Society. There was very great reason why they should give to the society much more support and sympathy than they had done in years gone by, in order that the men engaged in mission- ary work, and also in the distribution ot the Word of God, might be assisted in their labours. The customary votes of thanks concluded the meeting. -

YOIING THIEVES AT WIDNES.—A boy named Joseph Bright, 12 years of age, was brought before the Widnes' magistrates on Monday charged with stealing a pipe, the property of Elizabeth Waterson, of Mersey-rd. The prosecutrix has a stall in the Market Hall, and on the 6th 1 inst. the prisoner snatched up a pipe and ran away. He was afterwards captured by P.C. Massey. who dis- covered that the prisoner had thrown the pipe on the roof of Webb's public-house in Anne-st.—Bright, toget- her with Wm. Bushell, (13), Peter Connolly, (15), and Wm. Wallace, (14), was then charged with stealing four bottles of pickles, the property of Thomas Lawless, jam manufacturer, Warrington, from a stall in the Widnes Market. On the evening of the 6th inst. P.C. Holbrook met the three last named prisoners, each carrying a bottle of pickles. Inquiries elicited the fact that four bottles had been stolen from Mr. Lawless and the prison- ers were apprehended, and they made statements incrim- inating each other.—Bushell was also charged with stealing two tin money boxes, the property of Mrs. Waterson, of Mersey-rd.—The magistrates sentenced Bright to receive six strokes and Bushell three strokes with the birch rod, and Wallace was fined 10s.—Mr. Brock said Connolly had been three times before the Court, and evidently wanted saving from himself. He would have to go to goal for 14 days, and then be con- fined five years in a reformatory school. HARVEST FESTIVAL AiT ZION CHAPEL, WIDNES.— The annual services of thanksgiving for the harvest were held in Zion Vnited Methodist Chapel, Widnes, on Sunday. The edifice had been beautifully decorated with 'fruits, flowers, and cereals, and presented an attractive appearance. The pulpit was occupied, morn- ing and evening, by Mr. W. Brough, of Warrington, who preached two apprcpriate sermons. In the after- noon a service of song, entitled "The Harvest Festival," was admirably rendered by the choir and scholars, under_ the leadership of Mr. John Betney. Mr. A. Ogden was at the harmonium. The narrative was read by Mr. J. Showan. There was a good attendance at each service, and collections were taken in aid of the funds of the chapel. On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held, under the presidency of Mr. R. A. Naylor, of Warring- ton, who delivered an interesting speech. The choir rendered several pieces of music in good style. Miss Alice Betney was loudly applauded for her rendering of the song "When the tiae comes in," and Miss Green was very successful in the song "Dolly's revenge." Mrs. Locke sang with good taste "I dreamt I dwelt in marble halls," and this lady was associated with Miss Causey.in the duet "I know a bank." The duet *' They are waiting," &c., was given by Miss Smith and Miss Forrest. Miss E. J. Betney, Miss Harrison, and Mr. Robert Jenkins each gave a recitation. .4 intervals during the evening fruit was distributed, and a pleasant entertainment was brought to a close with the usual votes of thanks. The Chairman handed the Rev. E. Hall £2, to be added to the funds of the chapel. THE RENOWNED RUNCORN RELISH is prepared from the choicest herbs. roots, and spices, which render It of most valuable assistance in the digestion of fwd.—Prepared and sold wholesale by Isaac Stubbs. Lowland-road. Runcorn.— Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 20, 1888,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 20, 1888,

NEW RArs yoa HAvrox.--A rate for the township of , Halton, of 11d, in the pound, was signed on Thursday, at Runcorn, by Mr. J. Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst, the amount to be realized being £277 is. Sd. This is 3d. in the pound less than the rate made lot the previous hal f-year. Sr. PAUL'S CHURCH, WIDNES.—This church was beauti- fully decorated on Thursday evening, on the occasion of the Harvest Festival. The service was conducted by the Vicar (the Rev. G. H. S. Patrick Garrett) and the Rev. J. Connell, curate; while the Rev. Dr. Garrett, rector of Christ Church, Moss Side, Manchester, preached an appro- priate sermon: The choir, under the leadership of Mr. J. B. Imison,rendered the anthem "Ye shall dwell in the Land," in good style. The solos were rendered by Mr. T. Walker (bass) and Master Fred Martendale (treble). \ SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.-011 Monday evening, about six o'clock, a woman named Elizabeth Bradshaw, widow, 84 years of age, of Railway Bank Cottages, Farnworth, sat down with the rest of the inmates of the house to have her tea. he had not been sat there long before she complained of something coming up in her throat, as if she was golng to choke. She moved o the back door for the purpose of getting fresh air, and expired instantly. Dr. McLennan was called in to see the deceased, and was of opinion that heart disease was the cause of death, as he had attended her some months bqck for the same complaint. The Coroner considered an inquest unnecessary. DALTON SUNDAY SCHOOL *CIE CLUD.—A meeting of the Committee was held on Wednesday evening, in the girls' school, when there was a very good attendance of members. The Rev. J. Lockwood presided. The trustees, Mr. J. S. Jeacock and Mr. A. Povey, presented a state- ment of accounts, duly audited, which showed that there were some ninetS, members in the club, and a sum of £l4O 19s. 10d. in the Bank to its credit, besides a balance in the hands of the treasurer of £2 3s. 11d: £ll 2s. up. had been received in subscriptions during the nine months of 1888, £5 disbursed in sick payments, and £2 in funeral money. Miss A. Acton and Miss E. Watkin are secretaries. A CHILD BURNED AT WIDNES.—About half-past one on , Thursday afternoon, a girl, three years old, named Florence Underwood, daughter of Mr. s'arnes Underwood, grocer, 7, Witt-road, was playing by the side of a fire which had been made by some boys, behind the theatre, when her clothing caught fire. Police-constable Cumm- ing happened to be close by. and he wrapped the child in a coat and extinguished the flames. She had, however, been very severely burnt on the lower part of the body and thighs. The officer carried her home and applied linseed oil to the wounds. Dr. Robinson was afterwards called in and he dressed the wounds:- The girl is still in a serious condition. '_

RUNCORN PARISM CHIMICH HARVEST FESVVAL.—The annual thanksgiving service was held in All Saints Church on Thursday, evening. The edifice is well adap- ted for the di ay of the decorator's art, and the ladies of the congreelltion utilized the opportunity with artis- tic skill, and the general effect was very fine. There was a large congregation. The Vicar intoned the prayers, the first lesson was read by the Rev. W. Bryant, and the second lesson by the Rev. H. Wilcockson (Weston Point.) The Rev. Canon Gore, Archdeacon_ tof Macclesfield, preached an eloquent sermon. During the service the choir sang the anthem "Oh God, my soul thirsteth", the solos being taken by Master J. Hampson (treble), Mr. Kay (alto), Mr. J. Littler (tenor), and Mr. Caygill (bass.) CONVICTED ON A CHILD'S TESTIMONY AT WIDNES.—" I've three sons in gaol, and that's trouble enough," was the statement of Margaret O'Brien, from the prisoner's dock at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday. The woman was accused of stealing a red flannel singlet. and a child's frock, betonging to William Melton, of 37, Elizabeth-st., and the chief 'witness against her was a boy about six years of age, the son of the prosecutor. On Monday afternoon the boy was left in charge of the house • for three quarters of an hour, and he was positive in hp assertion that, during this time, the prisoner, whose back door is opposite that of Melton's, entered the house, and took from the table the articles named. The woman protested her innocence, and called Elizabeth Hopkins to Prove that she was at home at the time stated. P.C. Mercer proved, however, that Hopkins was drunk that afternoon, and Inspectol• Keighley said the prisoner was very drunk when apprehended. Remarking that the woman had evidently been on the "spree," the Bench imposed a fine of 205.,0r 14 days. FOREIGN MISSIONARY SOCIETY AT FRODSTIAM.—On Wed- nesday evening a public meeting was held in Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Frodsham, when Mr. Walter Robinson. of Overton, took the chair. in the absence of Mr. John S. Rimmer. the deputation being the Revs. W. Kendrew. of Runcorn, and George Hammond, of St Helens. The Rev. J. Shipham read extracts from the annual report of the society for the past year, from which it appeared that the income of the society had been £131,867 2s. 6d., whilst the expenditure amouti ed to £137,967 10s. 3d., showing a deficit of £6,100 7s. 9d., which with the amount deficient the previous year gives a total debt of £16,869 7s. 8(1. The Frodsham branch had contributed £BO 9s: 4c1., from the following branches of the Circuit:— Frodsham. £36 19s. 7d.; Kingsley, £l3 14s. Id. ; Helsby, £l3 ss. 10d.; Five Crosses. £l6 9s. 10d An amour* of £7 Vs. id. had also been received from the Frodsham branch, on account of the ladies' auxiliary mission. On the motion of the rev, gentleman, votes of thanks were passed to the Treasurer of the branch (Mr. W. C. Collin- ) and Secretary (Mr. Samuel Smith), and on his recommendation they were 1:9-appointed. The Rev. W. Kendrew and the Rev. G. Hammond delivered addresses on mission work. .

...„... RUNCORN CHURCH iNSTITUTE.—The Runcorn Church Institute was inaugurated by a concert, on Tuesday evening, in the National School, Church-st. A very good programme had been arranged, and a large and appreci- ative audience assembled to witness the proceedings. The first item on the programme was a glee, " Oh, who will o'er the downs so free," in which Messrs. Garner and Gates, and Misses Hampson and Howard, took part. A song, "Brother's Lament," by Mr. Harry Collins, was encored, a song by Miss Joynson was well rendered and was encored. Miss Isherwood favoured the Company with song" Romanze," Miss Simkin sang" The Soldiers's Dream," in good fashion, and being encored, sang ' " Dolly's Revenge." Miss Isherwood played a pianoforte , solo for which she was encored. The song "Good-bye," was well sung by Mr. Arthur, after which Mr. Harry Collins interpreted the comic sketch, "Mr. John Evan Thomas." After a short interval, the glee party sang "Where art thou, beam of light 2' " Martha" was given in a pianoforte duet by Mrs. Kay and Miss Isher- wood. " The Broken Picture" was next rendered by Miss .Toynson, and received an encore. After a banjo solo by Vr. Harry Collins, Mr. Williams sang" Love's Request," and ,receiving an encore,gave "The Distant Shore.' Mr. Piernnint's cornet solo was goad, and "The Better Land." by Miss Simkin, was nicely rendered. Miss Arg,ent's'violin solo, "Mazurka," was meritorious. Mr. ' Marwood's song, "The Lost Barque," was ably rendered. Mr. Wynne Humnhrevs played the accompaniments in conjunction with Mrs Kay. HARVEST FESTWAL AT ST. EDWARD'S, RUNCORN.— Special thanksgiving services for the harvest were held at St. Edward's Catholic Church, on Sunday last. The sacred edifice had been tastefully and appropriately decorated for the occasion. The pillars were entwined with ivy and ferns, and a profusion of flowers, fruit, and cereals adorned the communion and other parts of the church. A good congregation assembled in the morning, when IFligh Mass was celebrated. The musical portion of the service was rendered by a choir composed chiefly of members of the choirs of Lowe House and Holy Cross churches. St. Helens, and was a rich Anat. The soloists were. Miss Maud Dennett (soprano), Mr. Percy Barton (tenor), and Mr. Frel Dennett (basso). The orchestra comprised two Ist violins, two 2nd violins, flute or clarinette, cornet, trombone, 'cello, contra bass, and .drums. and WAS under the leadership of Mr. Wm. Gardner, of St. Helens. The organist was Mr. William Dennett, of Portico Chapel, near Prescot, and the con- ductor was Mr. H. M. Green. In the morning the music was Gonnod's Messi Solennelli, but the service was con- cluded by the Hallelujah Chorus (Handel). In the evening Benediction was celebrated, and thd church was filled. The serviee opened with Mr.FredDenriett render- ing "The Palms "(Hatton), with violin obligato by Mr. P. Shaw. During the offertory Mr. Percy Barton sang Zingarelli's " Laudate." Murphy's No. 2 Benediction Service was given, the band and chorus again giving the Halleluiah Chofus in conclusion. The Rev. Dr. Gas- taldi was the officiating priest. Love's YOUNG DREAM AT Wlnvizs —At Widnes Petty Sessions,on Thursday. Elijah Hewitt, of 6 West-st., West Bank. was summoned to show 'cause why he should not contribute towards the support of his wife. Mr. Knowles was for the plaintiff and Mr. Peters for the defendant.— Mr. Knowles said these young people were married in April of this year, the husband being 21 and the girl 19 years of age. Three days after marriage they began to " fall out." Defendant was jealous of his wife, and in consequence squabbles were continually taking place. On one occasion she WAS having a ride on the "hobby horses" at Ditton, and because he thought he saw her smile at somebody, he beeam4 enraged and said if she would go away he would give her 15s. a week to live upon. He is a furnace man at Messrs. 'Bolton's copper works, and earned 355. per week. On Monday, the 17th Sept.,defendant told his wife that he had taken a house at Appleton, and they must remove from James- at. Next day, while the wife was with her mother, he locked up the house and went away, and on that night the wife had to stop with a friend named Lily Weight. Next morning she borrowed a key from a neighbour, and entered the house. The defendant, on returning from his work, fetched a policeman to take her into custody for housebreaking. For several days the defendant kept away from the house, and provided no food for the wife. About 7 o'cleck one morning a lurry came to the door, the furniture was loaded upon it, and thewife was told to get out. Since that time the wife had lived with her mother: and the husband had done nothing to main- tain her.—Mr. Timmins and Mr. Gaskell remarked that it was a pity these young people should wreck their after lives by washing dirty linen in public, and suggested that they should confer and settle the matter between them. The couple wrt into the magistrates retiring room, and after a few minutes absence they returned, and it was stated that the husband had agreed to provide a home and they would live together.—The summons was therefore adjourned for a week.

SHOCKING OUTRAGE ON A CHILD AT RUNCORN.—Yester-

day morning the magistrates committed John Swift. a young man, employed as a tailor at Messrs. Unsworth's establishment, to the Assizes for trial on a charge of having on the 15th Oct., committed an outrage on Selina Martha! Bucl;le, aged 2 years and 9 months, daughter of

Betsy Buckle. POOR RATES FOR DITTON AND BOLD.—Mr. Houghton, assistant overseer, on Thursday applied to the Widnes magistrates to sanction the laying of a rate of Is. in the £ for the township of Ditton, for the ensuing half year. The rateable value of the township was £12,860 and the rate was estimated to produce £843 Os. ed. The arrears on the last rate were only £4 ss. and were recoverable. The magistrates sanctioned the rate. The Bench also agreed to the laying of a rate of Is. 4d. in the £ for the township of Bad, estimated to produce £1,153 3s The rateable value of Bold was £17,297. THE GOLDEN LION AT RUNCORN.—At Knutsford Quarter Sessions, on Tuesday, before Judge Horatio Lloyd, an appeal was heard, made by David Snell, land- lord of the Golden Lion, Runcorn, against the decision of the magistrates on the 13th August, when he was fined £4 and costs for harbouring prostitutes. The I decision of the magistrates was unanimously affirmed. A second case was heard •in which Snell appealed against the decision of the licensing justices acing for the Runcorn Division of Cheshire on September 24 in refusing the renewal of his license. This appeal wa:s also dismissed, with costs.

• 'CZ, STEALERS AT WIDNES.—Ada Reynolds (10), and Julia Wallace (9), were brought before the Widnes mag- istrates, on Thursday. charged with stealing 231bs of coal belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Co.—P.C. Murray deposed to haying seen the prisoners take the coal from near the crane on the can tl side, and place it into a box.—Mr. GaWell told the Mothers of the prisoners that the children had no doubt been sent to steal the coal ; it was not to the interest of" the children to steal coal. As this was the first case, a fine of only ss. would be imposed upon each defendant ; on the next occasion a fine would not be accepted.' WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions.onThursday,several persons were summoned by Mr. G. H. Hanby, clerk.to the school Board, for neglect- . . .

ing to send their children regularly to school. Ihe usual penalty of ss. was imposed in each case. Mr. Danby asked that Michael McPortland, who resided with his parents at 13 Pleasant-street, should be sent to an industrial school. His parents had been summoned 11 times befsre the Committee of the school Board, and had been II times fined by the magistrates. The boy was completely beyond control, and in the habit of sleeping out at nights.—The boy was committed to Beacon-lane Industrial School, Liverpool. PARAFFIN LAMP EXPLOSION AT WIDNES.—About two o'clock on Saturday morning, Catherine Farrell, a young woman, who lives at 41, Charlotte-st., attempted to blow out the light of a paraffin lamp, with the con- sequence that the oil was set on fire, and an explosion occurred'. The woman's hands, arms, face, and breast were very severely burned, and she ran into the street screaming loudly. Constables Ratcliffe and Porter happened te be in the vicinity, and at once applied flour to the wounds, to the woman's great relief. They afterwards obtained SORIP lime water and oil froM the works of Messrs. Muspratt, and with this the wounds were dressed. Dr. O'Keeffe has since .attended to the woman.

RUNCORN CASES AT QUARTER SEssmois:--On Tuesday, at Knutsford Quarter Sessions, the following sentences were passed :—Mine Hughes (30), musician, was sen- tenced to twelve calendar months imprisonment for stealing a blanket, the property .of Martin Gilligan, on the 22nd Sentember, at Runcorn. George Cleverley (72), labourer, was charged with stealing three gold and nine silver watches, three gold chains, eight silver chains, and eight gold finger rings, of which he was then the bailee, at Runcorn, on the 27th August, frona William Leach. Sentenced to nine months' imprisonment. Isabella Heath (60) was sentenced to be imprisoned for four calendar months for a theft of two pounds of mutton, the roper: .y of Mary Jane Hilditch, on the 31st August, at Runcorn. _ _ _ _

iNAHHOW ESCAPE AT Rmicorix.—On Wednesday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Dr. Steele and Mr. G. L. Wigg, a young man, named George Hayes, a well-known character, was charged with having stolen three hens, value 95., the property of George Duckett, lodging-house keeper, Church-st. The prisoner, and a woman named Mary Ann Walsh, had been living together as man and wife at Duckett's lodging-house. During that time five hens and four pigeons had been stolen from a cote in the yard, and no clue to the thief discovered. On Sun- day, the prisoner and his paramour quarrelled, and the woman accused tne prisoner of being the thief. Mary Ann Walsh now stated that she was drunk when she said the prisoner took the fowls.—Dr. Steele said be was of opinion that the prisoner did steal he fowls, but the evidence was not conclusive, and he would be dis- charged. SOUTH BANK BOWLING CLUB, Ruiscorcii.—The members of this club brought the bowling season to a close on Thursday evening, when upwards of 40 sat down to an excellent repast served in the dining hall of the South Bank Hotel. Afterwards Mr. T. Cooper, the president, occupied the chair, and Mr. John Coxhill the vice chair. The President gave the usual loyal toast, which was duly honoured Mr. J. Stubhs proposed "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," and Colour-Sergeant Coward and Quart,ermaster-Sergeant Hantinson responded. The toast of the • South Bank Bowling Club" was given by Mr. P. Smith, and acknowledged by the Vice-Chairman. "The Host and Hostess" were not forgotten, and Mr. Tom Jones suitably replied. In the course of the even- ' ing songs and recitations were given by Messrs. W. Wright, H. Johnson. S. Johnson, P. Smith, G. Slater, G. Turley, J. Widders, T. Price and others. Mr. J. Ravens- croft ably accompanied.

VIOLENT OUTRAGSE ON THE HIGHWAY, NEAR WIDNES.— At Widnes PettvoSessions, on Thursday, James Worrell, of Speke •' William Taylor, of Hale Cliff, Hale; Henry Taylor. ofHale ; and James Whyke, of Hale-road, Speke, were each charged with having caused grevious bodily harm to Thomas Burke, a dock labourer, of Garston. On Sunday af ernoon. Burke paid a visit to Hale village, and it was alleged that, when returning home about ten o'clock at night, slightly under the influence of drink, he was set upon by the prisoner Taylor and knocked to the ground. He was violently kicked about the head and body, and was severely injured. Shortly, afterwards, Constable Walker found Burke lying on the ground, and Wormll and Whyke standing over him. Both men were in drink, and he ordered them away. Acting on his advice, Burke commenced to walk towards Garston with the intention of getting his wounds dressed by a doctor, and the officer followed him at a distance. Burke had not proceeded far when the officer saw Worrell and ,ke spring from a gateway, and knock Burke down kick him. The constable at once apprehended forrall and locked him up.—Dr. Hutchinson deposed. that the prosecutor was in a very dangerous condition, and the prisoners were remanded for a4week. Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for three of the prisoners. VIOLENT ASSAULT IN A WIDNES BEERHOUsE.—Before Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, John Devlin, labourer, of 80, Midwood-street, and Catherine Devlin, barmaid at the Manchester beerhouse, Wellington-street, were brought up on remand charged with having caused grevious bodily harm to Arc.iibald Sullivan. labourer, of 9, Nelson-street It appeared that on the 2nd inst., Sullivan was in the beerhouse from u. o' clock in the morning until 2 p.m. At this time he was talking to the female prisoner, when her brother rushed at him, struck him a violent blow on the nail, and knocked him down. While he was lying on the floor, both prisoners kicked him. Sullivan scrambled to his feet, and went into the street ; the prisoners followed him and again kicked him; the woman threatening to finish him. It was alleged that there was no cause for this violence.' Dr. Hutchinson stated he had attended to Sullivan, who had been confined to bed for eleven days. His fare and body were badly bruised, and the fifth rib on the left side was broken.—Mr. Knowles, for the de- fence,callecl witnesses who stated that Sullivan had used foul language to the woman, and had struck her on the face. The brother then interfered, and Sullivan "invited him outside," and the latter received his injuries in a " fair stand up fight."—The prisoners were committed to take their trial at the next Quarter Sessions. CONCERT AND PRESENTATION AT APPLETON.—The anni- vennry ef the opening ef St. Bede's Boys' Schools was celebrated on Tuesday evening by a tea party and con- cert. In the early evening there was a numerous gather- ing in the schools, where an excellent tea was dispensed by the ladies of the congregation. Afterwards the com- pany adjourned fothe concert room to listen to a very interesting entertainment given by the members of the choir, assisted by Dr. McCambridge and Masters F. and C. Mercer. The following programme was gone through in capital style :—Song, "I would be a soldier still," Mr. F. Heyes; "Bally Hoolev." Mr. Morrison; pianoforte solo. "Harmonious Blacksmith," Master F. Mercer ; ballad, "Irish Emigrant," Mr. Caldwell; song, "Miss. Brady's pignofortay, ' Dr. McCambridge ; song, "Good bye, Sweetheart," Mr. Hanlan ; song, "I may or may not," Mrs. Heves ' • duet, "Singing lesson," Mrs. Caldwell and Mr. J. Caldwell; song, Mr. Finn; pianoforte duet, "Caliph of Bagdad," Masters F. and C. Mercer; song. "Tom Bowling," Mr. Reyes ; song, "1888," Mr. Morri- son; song, "Killaloe," Dr. McCambridge.—During the evening, the Rev. Father Cavanagh, formerly curate at St. Bedes, was presented with a valuable time piece from I the Young Men's Society, and a purse of gold from the congregation in recognition of his earnest and self-sacri tieing, services to the people of Appleton,to whom he had- greatly endeared himself. The presentation was made by Mr. Morrison, in an appropriate speech, and the very Rev. Dean Finigan also paid a tribute to the good quali- ties of Father Cavanagh, who suitably acknowledged the gifts. "TEE JOHN BULL" BOOT, twelve months' wear guaran- teed. A committee was formed for the purpose of getting subscriptions and carrying out the work, Mr. Henry Slatter being chairman, Mr. C. P. Scott, treasuitr, and Mr. J. H. Crosfield hon. ' secretary. Advt CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—At Warrington Police' Court on Tuesday Charles Renshaw, of the Albert Inn, Runcorn, was charged with having caused a horse to be ill-treated by having it worked when it was not in a fit state, on the Bth inst. Last week the driver of the horse was brought before the magistrates and discharged, the Bench expressing the opinion that the owner of the• animal should have been proceeded against. Henshaw,the owner, was in consequence summoned. From the evidence it appeared that the horse was employed in towing a load of timber up the Mersey, and when at War- rington attention was called to its condition. On being examined the animal was found to be suffer- ing from various ailments, and Dr. Robinson, veter- inary surgeon, deposed that it was totally unfit to be worked ;it was only fit to be destroyed. The magistrates said that they considered the case to be one of great cruelty, and imposed a fine of £2 and costs, in all .E 3 7s. 6d. It was stated that the horse had been destroyed.

DARRSBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.— A meeting of this Board was held in the court room, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. E. Greenall presided, and there was a full attendance of members. On the minutes of the previous meeting being read Mr. J. Derbyshire objected to the wording of a minute having reference to a proposal made at the previous meeting that proceedings be taken against him if he did not give up to the Board a quantity of pipes, &c., belonging to them, but which were stored on his premises. That proposal, he said, was never put to the meeting, and he objected to the manner in which it had been put on the minutes.— Mr. Aaron, in reply to the Chairman, said he had moved that action be taken against Mr. Derbyshire if the pipes were not given up. and Mr. Jones said he had seconded that proposal. The Chairman moved that the minutes be confirmed and this was agreed to.—lt was stated that letters had been received from Messrs. S. Chaddley and W. Long, with regard to the alleged encroachment in rappen- hall-road, and these were referred to the Committee ' appointed to deal with t`se matter.—Mr. T. Monks, of Walton Old Hall, wrote calling the attention of the Board to the condition of the road near his place, and the matter was referred to the Surveyor.— A letter was read from the surveyor (Mr. Peerman) stating that he intended applying for an increase of salary at the next Board meeting, and referring to the %Ara work that had been cast upon him by the ship canal works and the Liverpool water works at Norton. A committee was appointed to inquire into matters connected with this intended applica- tion,and to report to the next Board meeting. This was the principal business, in addition to some matters relating to tbe ship canal, which will be found reported along with our other ship canal news.

On Thursday evening a meeting of the Execu- tive Council of the Northwich Division Liberal Association was held at Mr. Fletcher's Office North- with. There were representatives present from each district in the division and Mr. H. Bratt presided in the absence of Mr. d. H.,Deakin, in London. Mr. W Handley, the Secretary, submitted a report on the registration wok. which was considered highly satisfac- tory and was heartily approved. It as decided that on the occasion of Earl Granville's visit to Manchester on the 2nd November, an address should be presented, to that nobleman, gm behalf of the Association.

A ROUGH SATURDAY NIGHT AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. John Brock and Mr. H. Gaskell junr., a young man named John Stewart, of Wareing-st., pleaded guilty to having been‘drunk and disorderly in Victoria- road, on Saturday, and also to having assaulted P.C. Rose. It was stated that the prisoner " wanted" to fight another man, and upon Constable Rose ordering him to go away he struck that officer on the face and chest with his fist, and violently grasped him by the throat. A struggle.ensued and the officer eventually took the prisoner to the police station.. For being drunk the prisoner was fined ss. and costs, or seven days, and 108. and costs or ten days for the assault.—John Coyle, a rough- looking man, of 3:1 Grenfell-st., Simms Cross, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and assaulted P.C. Foster. About five o'clock on Saturday evening the prisoner was drunk in Gran- fell-st., and was in the act of striking a man on the head with a poker, when the constable interposed and prevented the outrage. The prisoner then kicked the constable several times, and was at onae taken into custody. The services of several policemen were necessary to convey him to 'the police station. The prisoner was fined a total sum of 15s. and costs, or 21 days' hard labour.—Bridot McGuire,sister of the prisoner, was charged with resisting P.C. Forster whilst in the execution of his duty, and she was fined ss. and costs, pr seven days.—Richard Rawlinson, of Sutton's-lane, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly and further with assaulting P.C. Porter. About midnight on Saturday the prisoner was taken into custody on the first charge, and kicked and struck the constable in a violent fashion. He also bit one of the officer's fingers.—lnspector Keighley said the prisoner had been before the magistrates on seven occasions and he seemed to have a mania for assaulting the police.— The prisoner said he was 17 years of age when he first appeared before the Court. He had got into bad corn - pany and been led astray. He asked the Bench not to send him to gaol, as he did not wish to lose his situation. He was desirous of leading a better life, as he had lost his character. The prisoner was fined ss. and costs for being drunk, or seven days, and 20s. and costs, or a month, for the assault.—Selina Smith, who said she had come from Burnley, in search of her husband, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly and with having assaulted PC. Field. About eleven o'clock aatneonifaht gaegsonmeravmsadnrdunlpc.rdAreritiitiogoka her rstiiinrb-to custody. On the way to the lock-up the woman threw herself to the ground, and savagely kicked the constable on the legs. She was fined 12s. 6d. and costs t or. in default, 17 days' hard labour.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD,
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD,

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. R. Bradshaw presided and there were Present Dean Finegan. Dr. Olieeffe, Major Wareing, Messrs. F. Heyes, R. H. Davies, C. E. Bar- lbw, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

• DISTRICT EDUCATION. The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing September (4 weeks) there were 112 applications for school fees, which were recommended to be paid in 104 cases. There were 119 persons summoned before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act • and 32 were brought before the magistrates and convicted.— The minutes were adopted.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.-A TFACHEIS FINED.
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.-A TFACHEIS FINED.

The School Management Committee made the follow- ing recommendations :—That the indentures of Martha A. Dutton, a pupil teacher in the infants department of the Siniins Cross School, be cancelled at once and that the fine in this case be not enforced. That the resigna- tion of Miss Annie Winn, assistant mistress in the junior department of the Simms Cross school, be accepted. That Miss Edith Hirst be transferred from the senior girls' department, Simms Cross, to the, junior department at the same salary as she is at pre- sent receiving, viz. £45 per annum. That 25 percent. of the drawing grant earned by the scholars and the whole of that earned by the pupil teachers in the seniori boys departments for the year .ended August 31st, be paid to the teachers.—Dean Finegan moved the adoption of the minutes. In reply to Major Wareing and Dr. Ck'Keeffe, Dean Finegan declined to state in the

presence of the reporters what charge had been made against Martha Dutton. She had been married, mid this must not be taken as a dismissal—she had tendered her resignation.—Major Wareing said there • had been some charge made, and he understood that a doctor's • certifi- cate had been obtained. He should like to know if the doctor's certificate had substantiated the charge made against the girl.—Dean Finegan: As far as the doctor's certificate goes, I think that it is rather in favour of girl.—Major Wareing thought there ought to be a full niquiry,otherwise an injustice might be done to the girl. —Dean Finegan said the girt was not in school nor likely to be in school. The question was whether the Board would insist upon her coming back. He proposed that the indentures be cancelled.—The Chairman seconded. —Dr. O'Keeffe moved that ,he subject be inquired into by a Committee of the whole Board.—Major Wareing seconded.—Only two members voted for the amendment, and it was resolved that the isdentures he cancelled. After some further discussion it was resolved, on the motion of Major Wareing, Seconded by Dr. O'Keeffe,that the fine be imposed. The other minutes were passed. THE FINANCES. _

The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £705 Os. 9d., and reported that tile receipts for the past month amounted to £l,lBB 13s. Bd. The balance sheet for the half year ended September 29th was submitted.. The receipts amounted to £9,593 6s. 7d., and included balance on March 25th £225 15s. 6d.1 grants from Council of Edu- cation, Science, and Art Department £139 18s., pay- ments made to the .reasurer by ratin.„o. authorities £4,300, school , fees £905 Os. 7d., books and other- articles sold to children £4 14s. 2d., income from hire of room £l7 18s. 4d., loan from the Public Loan Board £4,000. The expenditure amounted to £5,058 Bs. The principal items were salaries of the Board £319 16s. Bd., legal and other expenses of administration £lll ss. id., salaries of teachers £2,635 is. 9d., books, apparatus, and stationery £126 4s. 9d., fuel, light, cleaning. kc., £298 Bs. 4d., rents, rates, taxes, and insurance £23 Bs., other expenses of maintenance £4l 14s. 7d., contribu- tions towards industrial schools £53 14s. 2d., by pur- chase of land and enlargement of school buildings £458 12s. 6d.. repayment of ptilicip.l of loans £269 5s id., and interest on loans £720 17s. id.. There was a balance in hand of £4,534 18s. 7d. The outstand- ing liabilities of the Board amounted to £35,772 175.10 d. The minutes were adopted.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
That thik Coroner was very severe in his remarks on the Widnes Police last week, and by those within, the inner circle his strictures are consider- ed uncalled for.

That the jaror was properly, summoned and the police were rot responsible for the erratic time kept by his clock; and that the law provides a means by which transgressors shall be punished. That the Constable left the Court to fetch the absent one, while the Sergeant went in search of a fresh juror?- What more could they do ? That Widnes, with one or two townships added, is entitled to send two representatives to the Lan- cashire County Council. That it is generally considered that the Chemical Metropolis, without any addition to its population, was large. enough and important enough to have two members, That what cannot be cured must be endured.
That great satisfaction is expressed that Runcorn, although ha ing only two-thirds of the population of Widnes, has been awarded two representatives to the Cheshire County Council. . . _ _ _

That it may ge taken for granted that the elections in these towns, and no doubt throughout the country, will be fought on political lines, and thus the ratepayers will have placed before them clearly defined principles of action.

That it is hoped that the interests of the people will be the aim of the county councils, and not, as under the present system, the interest of a class. That already it is given as a foregone conclusion that two Liberals will be elected for Runcorn,and the question "who will the gentlemen be "is being discussed. That Father Nugent is a grand specimen of a total' abstainer, and delivered a soul-inspiring speech to a. large audience of Runcornians on Tuesday evening, and made a deep impression upon many present. That it is devoutly to be wished that the good effect produced will be permanent. That Mr. P. Smith has been elected Chairman of the Baths Committee, and that the able Secretary to the Commissioners is obtaining all the necessary information for a complete discussion upon the advisability of* building baths. That a whisper is passing round that a proposal will be made at the next meeting of Use Board to increase the salary of the medical officer (Dr. McDougall) from £4O to 65 a year. _ _ _
That the-energetic, if rather eccentric, docter is wortl. all the money for the keen and watchful eye he keeps upon the health of the town.

CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES. Before HM Honour Judge Thompson, at Widnes County Court, on Saturday, George Johnson, of 19, Davies-street, brought an action against Joseph B. Aitkin, proprietor of the Salammoniae Works, Germrds Fold. Widnes, to recover £l5O compensa- tion for injuries sustained whilst in the defendant's employ. Mr. T. Swift, barrister, (instructed by Mr. Francis J. Poole, Widnes) represented the - plait:tiff, and the defence was conducted by Mr. Bradbury, barrister, Manchester, (instructed by Messrs. W.D. Jeans and Company, Warrington.). The plaintiff was employed as a labourer at the defend- ant's works, at an average weekly wage of 245. 6d., and he alleged that while working on the platform. in the ordinary course of his duties, he was over come by ammonia gas, slipped upon the platform, and rolled underneath the handrail to the ground. He fell a distance of 13 feet 6 inches, and was picked up in an unconscious state, his injuries in- cluding a fractured arm, a fracture of the base of the skull, and a general shock to the system. He was removed to the Accident Hospital, where he remained for a fortnight, under the care of Dr. Hutchinson and Dr. O'Neil, and he was afterwards an inmate of the Workhouse Infirmary for a num- ber of weeks. It was not denied that he would be unable to resume wont for a further period of three months. It was contended that the handrail, which. was 3 feet 6 inches Melt, was not sufficient protec- tion awl constituted a defect under the Employers Liability Act. The defence was that the action was to revive a person and not to cause insensibility, and that had it been otherwise, there was not suffi- cient quantity escaping to effect the plaintiff's con- dition. It was alleged that his insensibility arose through natural weakness, caused through want of food; that there was nothing of a dangerous char- acter in his occupation, and that the handrail was a sufficient. protection for the work carried on. A. number of scientific witnesses and.experts supported this view, and the Judge said a master could not be called upon to provide all the latest improvements in protective measures—he was merely to provide reasonable protection, and, looking at the nature of the plaintiff's work, he considered the handrail sufficient. He was also of opinion that the plaintiff was not overcome by gas. A verdict was given for the defendant, and Mr. Bradbury did no ask for costs.

On Wednesday Father Wadden received many tele. rams from admirers at home and in England congratula- ting him on his release from prison, and seyerartokens of regard were presented to him by inhabitants of Derry., ALARMING FIRE IN WEITRCHAPEL.—An alarming fire broke out about ten minutes to two o'clock on Thursday morning in 96, Leman-street, Whitechapel, a Jewish Co-operative Store, kept by Marcus Landon, a Polish Jew. Much excitement was caused in the neighbour- hood when it was known that Landon, his wife and nine children,were all sleeping on the top floor. Sergeant Gavrard and Constable 35 11 were among those first on the spot, -and they immediately rushed up the staircase and succeeded in bringing down the occupants before they had sustained any injuries. 'rhe chitchefi, along with an old female servant who was with some difficulty rescued, were taken to an adjoining house. A SINGULAR INCIDENT IN THE LIFE OF ONB OF OUR CITIZENS. • [rark Daily Herald, October 2nd.11 To the Editor.—Sir,—To my'many friends in all parts of Ireland, as well as other parts of the world, a short history of an incident in my life will no doubt prove interesting, and I sincerely hope, profitable. In 1883, while engaged as engineer of the s.s. " Vvelyn," I first found that I was not a well man. I had severe pains in the small of my back ; my head -ached almost constantly and I began to lose appetite and energy. When I hejd finished the voyage and re- turned to Cork, ; called on one of the very best medical practitioners in the city, but as I found I as receiving no benefit I soon stopped his attendance. Gradually, but most surely, I grew worse, and was forced to call in another eminent surgeon, and one holding a high official and professional position. He gave me some medicine which mademe much worse from the start, and cause.' blotches and pimples to break out over my face and body, and almost entirely destroyed my stomach. He thought my case a very serious one, and one, likely to result fatally. By this time I had become very greatly weakened; could scarcely walk, weak pulse, ft,p-rt, tongue, bad taste in the moilth, appetite almost entirely gone, greatest difficulty in retaining the simplest kind of nourishment on the stomach, and the old pains in the head and back were increased threefold. At one moment I would be cold as ice, and would get as close to the fire as possible, and the very next moment my skin would become hard and dry and every drop of my blood seemed like boiling water coursing through my veins. 1 called in, in succession four other of the best and most successful medical men in Cork, and spent not less than one hundred pounds in advice and medicine, but could get no relief whatever, I was fatally forced to take to my bed, and could not attend to any sort or kind of business, mental or otherwise. Every pain from which I had before suffered was increasing. My stomach, feet, and ankles became swollen and dropsical ; my memory became treaoherous -, I had given up all hope of ever regaining health', and only awaited death. One day I picked up, quite accidently from the bed, where my little niece had lefi it, a book in which my case was most accurately described, and at the same time giving instances of such eases being cured by "Warner's SAFE Cure." Haling lost all faith in the regular practitioner's methods of treating me, I decided to try it, and to that end at once procured a bottle, and then a second one, and by the time I had taken the second I felt that I had received some benefit. I wrote to Messrs. Warner Co. in London, and from them got some advice about my diet, drink, and baths. I- took the medicine honestly according to directions, and followed stric ly the diet, as well as observed to the letter the advice received privately from the firm. I had wasted away until -I only weighed 8 stone 1 lb., and in twenty-two days I weighed 8 stone 9 lbs., a gain of 8 lbs. in three weeks, and this was the very least part of my improvement in the same time, for my pains were rapidly leaving me, my appetite and digestion were improving, and the change generally was so radical that my friends and family were simply astounded The improvement continued until I had taken more than thirty bottles of the "Warner's SAFE Cure," and 'found myself thoroughly and absolutely cured, and I thank God for the medicine, and for the fact that after five years of the most intense suffering lam to-day as strong and healthy as at any time in my life, and capable of doing any kind of work. I began taking the "War- ner's SAFE Cure" in December last, and in less than six months it did more for me than six of our best medical men could do in q years. lam glad to heartily recom- mend "Warners SAFE Cure" to all sufferers from Kid- ney. Liver, or Bladder disease, and I give this testi- monial out of gratitude for the benefit I have received from the medicine, and I hope its widespread publication may prove of benefit to others afflicted as I have been. At one time I was reported dead, and neighbours closed their shops out of respect for me. 1 Yours faithfully, Was. MURPHY.
No. 1, George-st., Cork, Sept. 27th.
POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROtIGH POLICE COURT. SATTIRDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. BEctonm.—A woman named Sarah Harris was sent to gaol for seven days, for having asked alms in Horsemar- ket-street on the previous night. MONDAY .—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton) Alder- man Harrison, Councillors Greening and J. Pierpoint. DRUNKSNNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence.—Robert Evans, in Irla,m-street, on Saturday night, fined ss. including costs ; James Spices, in Tanners-lane, on Sunday afternoon, fined ss. and costs ; John Bibby, in Bridge-street, on Sunday night, fined ss. and costs • William Hughes, in Dallam-lane, the same morning, fined 5s and costs ; Timothy Burns, in Old-road, Latchford, on the 6th inst., fined ss. and costs ; James Dakin, in Irlam-street, on the 7th inst., fined ss. including costs ; and Jane Barber, in Butter- market-street, on the 7th inst., fined ss. including costs.

tHIMNET ow FIRE—For having allowed the chimney of his dwelling house to be on fire, on the 10th inst., Thomas Davies was ordered to pay Is. SUSPECFED.—A young man named John Rooney was brought up on a charge of having been found on the premises of George Pilling, publican, Bridge-street, on Sunday night, where it was suspected he had gone for the purpose of committing a felony. Defendant explained the matter to the satisfaction of the magis- trates, who dismissed him. A VIOLENT CUSTONER.—Anthony Gibbons, a labourer, was charged with having been drunk at the Rodney Inn, , with having refused to quit the premises when requested to do so, and with having assaulted the barman, Simeon ' Smith. He was fined ss. and costs. OBSTRUCTIONISTS.—WiIIiam Timmins and Edward Bil- lington were summoned for having caused an obstruc- tion in Market-street, on the 10th inst., by allowing ' 4herses and carts to remain there an unreasonable time. They were each fined 10s. including costs.—Samuel Bennett, for a similar offence, was ordered to pay the Cogs. OVERCROWDING.—George Marsh, 7 Pilkington's Court, off Fennell-st., was summoned for taking lodgers, on the 10th inst., without having his house registered. When the house was visited defendant, his daughter, aged eighteen, a woman named Coyne, and a child, were found to be occupying the same bed. Alderman Harri- ton said that a more gross case of indecency he had hardly ever heard of. A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed. or a month's imprisonment in default Of Paymen. Scnoot Casas.—The following cases under the Elementary Education Act were brought before the Bench, Mr. George Riley prosecuting on behalf of the School Attendance Committee :—Elizabeth Moores, Cockhedge-lane. Boy ordered to be sent to the training ship Clio.—Peter Hanlon hawker, Silver-square, fined 55.; John Stringer, Hanlon, fined 2s. 6d.; William Lloyd, forgeman, Orford-lane (two cases), fined 2s. 04, in each case; Patrick Corfield, Vere-street, fined ss. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. J. Guest and.R. W. Francomb. ' Daurntami•ess.—ThowiA Williams, a painter, was finedl ss. including costs for having been drunk in Ashton-st. on Monday evening. Scuoot Cases.—James Tickle, railway employe, Aikin- st., was fined ss. for neglecting to send his child to I school. The boy had only made 17 out of a possible 120 attendances.—ln the case of Richard Ridgway, Howard- at., the Bench made an order for the lad to be sent toi the Clio. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough,Alderman Chandley, and Mr. R. Garnett. DRUNIERNSIESS.—For this offence John Welsh, farm labourer, was fined ss. and costs, and a similar penalty was imposed upon a woman named Maria Gallagher. Ann Raw, housekeeper, Daresbury, who was found help- lessly drunk in the Market Place on the previous night, and WU taken to the police station in a handcart, was released on payin; the lock-up fee, one shilling. THE EDUCATION ACT.—Michael Coffey was summoned for not having sent his boy, Richard, regularly to school. On the application of Mr. George Riley, school attend- ance officer, the magistrates ordered that the boy be sent to Father Nugent's Industrial School at Liverpool. TRURSDAY.—Before Major Litton, Alderman Webster, and Councillor Greening. DRUNICENNESS.—MichaeI O'Hare, who was charged with this offence, was dismissed with a caution. . FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison, Dr. Gornall,and Mr. Garnett. DRUNKENNESS—Mary Ann Fudge, for having been drunk and disorderly in St. James's-st., was ordered to pay Is., the lockup fee. MAINTENANCE —Michael Flynn Was ordered to pay is. a week towards the maintenance of his son in St. Ann's Industrial School, Liverpool.—Henry Sherwood was ordered to pay is. a week for the maintenance of his son on the ship Clio. OYERCROWDING.—Mary Coyne, 7 Pilkington's-yard, who in another case was fined 20s. and costs for drunkenness, was summoned for having kept lodgers on the 17th inst. without having her house registered. A fine of 20s. and costs, or, in default, imprisonment for a month, was imposed. DISORDERLY WOMEN.—Mary Coyne, Mary Lee, Jane Hewitt, and Mary Swift were charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Dial-st. on the 13th inst. The chief constable (Mr. Hunt) said that Dial-court and Rose- yard were the worst spots in Warrington. He asked for a substantial penalty to be imposed. The magistra es fined each defendant 20s. and costs, or, in default of pay- ment, imprisonment fora month. THEFT OF Mar.—Richard Condon, a Ship Canal labourer, was charged with having stolen 281bs. of mutton, value 195., from the shop of William Gill, butcher, Bridge-st., on the previous day. He pleaded guilty,isdad was sent to prison for two months, with hard 13IIIIIIr. GED WIFE ASSAULT.—James McCarthy was s ned for having assaulted his wife,on the 17th inst. milli On p mising to live comfortably with her, and pay the costs of the case, defendant was discharged.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Tinsley, W. H. Bleckly. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—John Murphy, on the 6th inst., at Croft, fined ss. and costs; John and Thomas Cunning- ham, on the 7th inst., at Croft, each fined ss. and costs; Samuel 'Terry, on Bth September, at Warrington, fined ss. and costs.

MISCELLANEOUS.—For allowing three cows to stray at Great Sankey, Joseph Crosby was ordered to pay 3s. and costs.—Sarah Little was summoned by Catherine Roger- son for having usd threats towards her. Mr.' H. J. Longton appeared for the defence.—Defendant was bound over to be of good b3haviour for three months.

div.p: FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. P. Stubs, H. Stanton, and C.
Lister.

ABSCONDING.—There was a summons against James Rabbit for having been drunk and incapable on the 7th bast., but it was stated that the defendant had absconded, and the case was adjourned for a month. A Dot; CASE.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed on Alexander B. Cheyne, Agden, for having kept a dog without a license.

ALTERATION TO A PUBLIC-HOUSE.-All application was made on behalf of Mr. Millwood, occupier of the Bull's Head Inn, Lymrn, for permission to make certain altera- tions to the premises.—The Bench granted the nerPssary permission. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE AT LYHM. - Peter Forster, of Lymm, who did not appear, was summoned for not-hav- ing sent his child regularly to school. The case had been adjourned from the previous Court-to allow defen- dant the opportunity of sending kis child more regularly. but it was stated by the Attendance Officer- that the child had been absent 15 times since the previous Court day.—Mr. Stubs said he had seen a letter in the "Times" the other day, that if a child was a few minutes late in going to school it was marked down as absent. He wished to know if that were so ?—The Attendance Offi- cer said the school was opened at nine o'clock and if a scholar was not there by ten o'clock it was marked as absent.—Mr. Stubs said it seemed to be quite fair enough.—A fine of 5s including costs, was imposed. . .

A EAZY VAGRANT .—An old nien nanied Brazendale was charged with having slept in a kiln at High Leigh Brick Works the previous night. It was stated that the pri- soner was in the habit of hanging about Broom Edge, when he was out of the Workhouse. Mr. Lister re- marked that he seemed to be an able-bodied man, but it was stated that he would not work. Prisoner promised that he would go to the Workhouse, and he was dis- charged. LEAVING WITHOUT Mmes.—James Webster, of San- key, who did not appear, was summoned by James Barker, thrashing-machine owner, for having left his employ without notice, and a claim of £2 16s. was also made against defendant, the items of which were made up as follows :-355. loss sustained through defendant leaving his work without notice and thus preventing the "tackle" being used for a day; 18s. for a week's wages in lieu of notice • and 3s. for the day's wages of a man who had to be engaged through defendant's leaving. Mr. Barker said that, the agreement between him and defendant was that a week's notice was to be given on either side. or in default of this, a week's pay, 18s., to be forfeited.—The Bench considerel that accor- ding to this agreement defendant could only claim 18s., but they were willing to adjourn the case in order that complainant might engage a solicitor to argue the point. This was agreed to by complainant, and the case was adjourned for a month.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT. Morn:ult.—Before Mr. John Brock, and Mr. H. Gaskell junr.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. Morn:ult.—Before Mr. John Brock, and Mr. H. Gaskell junr.

DRUNKENNESS.—John Starkey made his 46th appear- ance and was fined 10s, and costs for being drunk and disorderly. John O'Neil was fined in a similar sum, and Walter Bushell, 12th appearance, was ordered to pay ss. and costs ; Thomas Gray was mulcted in a similar sum. AN ABSENT MILITIAMAN.—Henry White was fined 40s. and costs, or seven days' hard labour, for being absent from the training of the 3rd Lancashire Regiment in April last. Titer'. AT SPEXE.—John Dwerryhouse, an old man. was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour for haying on the 9th inst stolen 381bs. of potatoes, the property of Mrs. Margaret Stockton, of Hale-road, Speke. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. H. Gaskell, jun. DRUNK.— Mary Ann Noon of Water-st., was fined 7s. 6d. and costs for being drunk and disorderly.

THURSDAY.—Before Mr.H. Gaskell jun., and Mr. T.
S. Timmins..

DIWNKENNESS.—Frank Harris, Major Cross-street. and Thomas Ramke, of Albert-street, were each fined 7s ed. and costs for drunkenness,and William Lowe, of Runcorn, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk at Ditton. Doo AT LARGE.—John Kennedy, of Margaret-street, was fined ss. and costs for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled.

RUNCORN POLICE C01:13T. SATURDAY.—Befdte Messrs. G. L. Davies and G. Lloyd Wigg. THE BEGGING NIIISANCE.—Evan Wilson, for begging is Wellington-st., on the previous day, was sent to gaol for seven days.—Thomas Larney, a tramp, was charged with a similar offence, in Lord-st., on the 12th bast. Pri- soner, who was an old man, was discharged with a caution.

Navvias IN TUOUBLE.—Joseph Green awl William Stnith, navvies were charged with having been found sleeping in a shed at the Delph on Friday night. The men were found in the shed shortly before midnight, asleep. On being roused they were taken into custody, and were each sew to gaol for seven days.—John Totty, also a navvy, was fined lOs and 7s. 4d. costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, for having been drunk and dis- orderly in Devonshire-place, on the 12th inst. He went to goal. DAttgitanntss.—Jane Eccleston, a feeble old woman. was fined ss. and costs for having been drunk in High-st on the previous day. WEDNESDAY.—Before Dr. Steele and Mr. G. Lloyd Wigg. A DESERTIM—DanieI Ward, a young man, pleaded guilty to having on the 2nd May deserted from Her Majesty's ship Northumberland at Portsmouth. He was ordered to be handed over to the ship Eagle, now lying in Liverpool Docks.
