Secretarfes of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bev sey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning

(RUGBY.) Garins Wax EXCIILSIORS V. REWSEV.—This match was played at Bewsey on Saturday. tke visitors winning easily. Score—Excelsiers 3 tries 8 minors, to nil. SUTTON " A" v. HALTON lst.—This match was played. at Sutton on Saturday and resulted in a win for the home team by one goal, two tries, and four minors to one goal. Moss BANK V. GLOBE RECREATION (2nd Teams.)— Played at Moss Bank last Saturday, and after a splen- didly contes ed game resulted in favour of the home team, who scored four minors to Globe Rees nil. Moss BANK V. HIONFIELD (A team).—These teams met at Highfield last Saturday in the presence of a fair con- c,eurse of spectators. The result was as follows : Highfield one dropped goal and one minor, to Moss Bank one try and five minors. WIDNES V OLDHAM, "A " TEAIRS.—A very interesting match was played by the two teams on Saturday, on the Lowerhouse-lane ground, before a good number of spectators, and resulted in a win by Widnes A, 1 goalt try, 4 minors, to Oldham, 1 try. only, WIDNES Sr. MARY'S V. Sr. HELENS RECREATION A.—A very exciting game was played between the above teams on Saturday, which was witnessed by a fair number of spectators. The game ended in a draw, the score stand- ing, St. Mary's 2 minors, to Recreation 3 minors. HALTON V. SurroN A TEAM.—This match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter. After a very tight game Halton won ley 1 goal 1 minor to Sutton 2 tries 4 minors. Foster scored the try for HaV.on, after a splendid run by Evans from his own twenty-five, Clucas kicking the goal. %Fumes 214 D V. FRODSEIAM —This match was played on Saturday at Frodsham, before a large crowd of specta- tors. Frodsham had decidedly the best of the play, the ball being kept nearly the whole of the time in the centre of the field or in the Widnes 25, a very exciting game resulting in a win for Frodsham by one goal to one minor.

MERSEY MISSION v. HILTON JOCKEYS.—PIayed on the ground of the latter, in grand weather, and ended in a win for the Mission by two tries and four miners to three minors. W. Russell and S. Cunliffe scored the tries, Hough failing at goal both times. For the Mission, S. Hough, S. Conliffe, T. Jones, C. Garrett, Russell, at back, and T. Jones and E. Kay, forwards, and for the Jockeys Hassell, Bowman, Humphreys, Fowler, played well at backs, and F. Crowther forward. SUTTON RECREATION v. WARRINGTON GRAMMAR Schoot.—Played at Sutton on Saturday. Play was confined to the centre until half-time arrived with the score Grammar School two minors, Recs one minor. In the second half Jos. Clarke scored a try, and A. John- son kicked a goal. Before time was called, A. Johnson getting possession, dropped a splendid goal, leaving the home team victors by two goals and five minors to Grammar School three minors. Sr. HELENS RECS. (A Ti) v. WIDNES ST. MARY'S. —Played at Widnes. Holt (the Rec's captain) lost the toss, and kicked off against the wind. The play vas very interesting during the first half and half-riffle arrived with the score Widnes St. Mary's one minor, Recreation nil. From the restart, the Rees took play into Widnes twenty-five. Roberts got hold and made a drop at goal, the ball just going outside the post. This gave the Rees their first minor. Some tight scrimmages took place in mid-field, neither aide having any advantage. When the whistle blew for time the score stood: Recre- ation three minors to Widnes one minor. SUTTON v. WARRINGTON ST. PAUL'S.—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday and ended hi a draw—Sutton a try and a minor to St. Paul's one try. The Sutton forwards went off with a rush, play being confined to the home team's quarters where a series of

scrimmages took place. From a scrim Age in the home twenty-five, W. Harrison obtained possession and mak- ing a neat and accurate pass to Twist, that player dodged his opponents in grand style and grounded the ball over the line near to the touch-in-goal, Bickerstaffe failing from a very difficult position. This was the only score in the first half, and in the second, the home team scored a try, no goal resulting. No other points being registered, the match resulted in a draw.

, WARRINGTON 2ND V. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS IST.— This match was played on Saturday, at Warrington' in beautiful weather. During the first half, Warrington, after some good passing, scored one try,Warburton, who got the try, failing at the plaee. In the second half, the game was very even, good play being shown on both sides throughout the match. A very good game ended in favour of Warrington by ltry and 5 minors,to Birken- head 1 minor. Rowe, Speakman, and Carson, backs, Teare, Beard, Lowton, and Warburton forwards, for Warrington, and Hurst, Cash, Hosk, Jones, and Suther- land for the Wanderers, played best. Teams :—Warring- ton, Carson back ; Boardman, Speakman, Lawless, three- quarters; Rowe and Mather, half backs ; Teare (capt.), Lowton, Beard, John and James Coyne, Warburton, Wood, Neil, and Howarth. forwards. Birkenhead ;—T. Bowyer, back; Norsworth, Hoak, and Cash, three- quarters ;`E. Hurst (capt.),and Herbert half back; Jones, May, Sutherland, G. J. and T. Garner, Watson, Bowyer, Barge, forwards. RUNCORN RECREATION V. LIVERPOOL 4TH L.A.V.— Played at Runcorn on Saturday in capital weather, before 500 spectators. At the outset the game was chiefly forward, the Recreation having the advantage and keeping the play confined to the visitors' territory. Houghton had twice hard lines in dropping at goal. From line out JOnes got a try. Shortly afterwards the Volunteers retaliated and scored a minor. This was the total score at half-time. In the second half the Volun- teers played up better And pressed their opponents, a good dribble being put% and infringement of the rules only prevented a score. By similar play Recreation visit- ed the Volunteers' goal-line, but good kicking relieved. Fair passing was now shown on both sides without result. Aftel.wards Recreation missed a good opporsun- ity, and the Volunteers by good following up compelled the home team to touch down. On kicking out Speak- man put in a good run, and was only brought down on the line. From the scrimmage Acton got a try. Score. Recreation, 2 tries, 2 minors, Volunteers,2 minors. Wirms v. OLDHAM.—The return match between these clubs, both of whom had their strongest teams, was played at Oldham on Saturday, before 3,000 spectators. The game was splendidly fought from start to finish,' and resulted in a victory for Widnes by 2 goals and 8 minors to 1 try and 2 minors. In the first half Widnes played against a strong wind, but, notwithstanding this dis- advantage, they quickly showed which was the best team. A few minutes frm the start, Farrell crossed the home line in capital style, and deposited the ball behind the posts. The same player landed a beautiful goal. Widnes continued to have the upper hand, and ultimately the home men relieved by kicking dead. Again the home territory was invaded. A scrimmage ensued in front of the posts, arid Farrell passed to Parkinson, who dropped a splendid goal. At half-time the score stood :—Widnes 2 goals 1 minor, Oldham nil. With a change of ends, the visitors did not maintain their form, while Oldham improved greatly. Johnson ran in and grounded the ball near ,he touch flag. Barlow failed to place a goal. Subsequently the home men added two minors. Now, however, the Wednesians pulled themselves together again, and time after time the home citadel was jeopardized, but the defensive tactics of the Owdamites " succeeded in preventing Widnes scoring. Thus the game closed as above stated. The above was very disheartening to the Oldham supporters, especially as Widnes beat them at Widnes, a few weeks ago. Widnes had the 'advantage at all points, Plumpton, Parkinson, Farrell, Wilkinson, Smith, and Kiddie play- ing a good game. Teams :—Widnes: S. Bingham, back: Plumpton (captain), Parkinson, Wright and Clarke, three-quarter backs ; Tamil and Wilkinson, half backs.; Smith, Inddie, Barber, Gaudy, Williams, _Holt, Gordon, _

..._, and Johnson, forwards ; Oldham: Barlow, back; Greaves, Mills (captain), and Logan. three-quarter backs ; Thomas and Moseley, half-backs; Armstrong, F. W. Lees, Vigram, Wolstencroft, Beetham, Mallalieu, Whitehead, and Johnson, forwards. .

Ma. T. R. Surrox's TEAM V. Wrimrs.—The annual ma ch between these teams took place at Whines on Thursday. The weather was all that could be desired, and a large attendance of spectators assembled to witness the encounter, which was exceedingly well contested throughout. A start was effected by Groves kieking off, and the visitors immediately forced their way into their antagonist's quarters. The game had only been in progress a few in minutes when Greene picked up and dashed over the opposing line, but Wain- wright failed to improve the position. Encouraged by this early success, the visitors played up with remarkable dash, and severely harrassed the rival defence, with the result that Oswald passed to Seddon, who dropped a capital goal. The visitors, however, still kept up the pressure, but eventually Widnes suc- ceeded in clearing their lines and had the satisfaction of placing their opponents on the defensive, but, unfor- tunately, Parkinson at this period of the game had to retire, owing to an accident. On resuming, Widnes could not long maintain the advantage gained. and Hurst effected a brilliant run down the field, the visitors registering a couple of minors in quick succession. At half-time Mr. Sutton's team were leading by a goal and a try to nothing. On changing ends Widnes went into the game with great determination, but brilliant play on the part of Brazendale, Hurst, Oswald, Greene, Faulkner. and Groves frustrated all their efforts. Ultimately Hewett gained a try, but Riddle failed to improve the point, and Widnes retired defeated by one goal, one try, and six minors, to one try and six minors. Teams t— Mr. T. R. Sutton's Team.—J. Brazendale (Runcorn), back : T. Smith (Leigh), R. Seddon (Wigan) R. Whitehead (Radcliffe), and J. Hurst (Leigh), three- quarters; J. Oswald (Free Wanderers) and J W. Edge (Broughton Rangers), half-back*; G. Wainwright (Run- corn), Faulkner (Runcorn), E. Wardle (Wigan), W. Dillon (Warrington), R. H Greene (Free Wanderers). R. Robinson (Broughton Rangers), J. Groves (Rochdale Hornets), and A. Wheeler (Birch), forwarde. Widnes.— S. Bingham. back; J. Hartles, J. Parkinson, J. Clarke, and J. Mallison, three-quarters; T. Wilkinson and J. Farrell, half-backs; W. Kiddie, F. Williams, E. Gordon, G. Hewett. J. Johnson, J. Gandy,. J. Smith, F. Wright, and R. Johnson, forwards. Itrumoior v. laavON-ON-Tantrr.—The Runcorn team

paid theirfirst visit to the Midlands on Saturday. Un- fortunately, owing to the Cheshire trial game' fiVe of the principal players could not accompany, the team. An early start was made before a large number of spectators by Evershed kicking off for Burton ,and the home players following well up, forced the visitors to save in the first minute of play. Shortly after the drop out Evershed tried to drop at goal, the ball falling short. Hughes passed to Lunt, who gained a little ground, but Ever- shed returned by a neat run to Runcorn 25. Broady came to the rescue, and Hughes made a spiendidkun to the home quarters, but Sully returned. Hugh. lORk.gsin getting hold, passed to Riley, who got in a nice run, when Eddy was forced to save at a critical time. Broady returned the kick out, and Riley, Gayter, and Hancock following well up again • forced Burton to save. Soon after the drop out the home team were forced backup:in their lines, and had a very narrow escaoe,. Eddy just saving in time. Some Severe scrimmaging followed the kick out, and some grand passing I was shown by Hughes, Crompton, and Riley ' for Runcorn, and Evershed, Sully, and Richard son for Burton, the last,named making his mark in the Runc,orn 25, the visitors being forced to save. Half ti nse was soon afterwards called, the score standing at four minors to two in favour of the visitors. During the second half the same fast and exciting play was wit- nessed on both sides, and some grand passing was Indulged in. Neither side could claim much advantage, the ball travelling from one end of the field to the other. Ultimately, a scrimmage being formed in the Burton 25, Hollingworth getting hold, passed back to Crompton, who dropped a splendid goal. Evershed restarted, and the home team strove hard to equalize, but could not cross the visitors' line. Tithe was now fast drawing to a close, and the game was still full of excitement, when P. Riley getting hold got in a splendid run to the visitors line, but Eddy checked his progress, and losing posses- sion of the ball, Dolan, being well up, picked up and crossed the line, Crompton kicking a good goal. No side was now called, and a grand game ended in a Vin for Runcorn. Final result :—Runcorn, two goals and six minors ; Burton, four minors. The following were the visiting team :—Runcorn: S. Booth, back • W. A. Riley, J. H. Crompton, and E. Lunt, three-quarter backs; H Hughes and J. Hollingworth, half-backs; W. H. Broady, P. Riley, J. Gayter, F. Hancock, R. Dolan, A. Harnpson, E. Andrews, J. Gatley, and J. J . Bowyer. forwards. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER FREE WANDERERS (" A" TEAMS) .—These teams met at Warring on on Saturday, before a fair number ef spectators. The visitors won the toss, and Isherwood kicked off for Warrington from the railway end. Molyneaux took play into the visitors' half, and the home forwards dribbled over the line, the full back saving. The Warrington forwards soon forded the visitors to defend their line, Vipond relieving slightly. Passing between J. Bate, Lawless, and Daniels took place, the latter player being collared by Goldthorpe. The Warrington forwards, by a smart dribble, again took the ball over the line, only to see the visitors save by touching' down. Gowan dropped out and play rested in the centre. The home forwards, headed by Isherwoed, Donoghue, and Bate, transferred play to neutral ground, where Holmes picked the ball from a loose scrimmage, and after a good run gained a try near the posts, J. Bate converting the point into a goal. Adamson and Donoghue forced another minor point from the drop out. The home forwards, who fairly outplayed their opponents, again placed the visitors on the defensive, Lawless passing to J. Bate, who took a drop at goal, the ball going just wide of the posts. Sanson scored two minor points from long kicks then Isherwood broke away from a line out and pa's;ed to Lawless, who kicked, and the forwards following up, Donohue dribbled the ball over the line, but the try was disallowed. Lawless next got nicely away from a scrimmage, but was collared by Gowan near the line, the visitors conceding another minor. Moly- neaux charged down the drop out, Bate preventing any return. J. Bate next gave Daniels a nice pass, the latter player running in a try, Isherwood kicking a splendid goal from a difficult position. 'On call of half

time Warrington was leading by two goals and nine minor points tO the Free Wanderers nothing. On change of ends Anderton restarted for the Free Wan- derers, Daniels returning well. Adamson put in a good dribble from a line out, but Goldthorpe returned into touch. Bibby returned the ball into touch in the visi- tors' 25, Molyneaux getting over the line, but the ball was ruled back, and the Free Wanderersworked the oval Ito centre. Sanson getting possession made a splendid run, rounding his men in fine style, and gained a try near the touch flag, Isherwood failing at the place kick'. A strong run by Lawless again took Operations to the visitors' 25, Isherwood running in• another try. the same I player taking the place kick but Wino. to augment the I point. J. Warrington continued to have the best of the game, and from a scrimmage in the Free Wanderers' 25, W. Heyes scored another try, no goal resulting. Anderton; three- quarter backs, Goldthorpe, Gowan, and Vipond ; half backs, Howard and Duck; forwards, Moir.. Hulme, Edwards, W. H. Anderton, E. Anderton, Haverfield,. Betney. Meagher, and another.
WARRINGT-ON V. MANCHESTER FRAE WANDERERS.

The first-mentioned team made their second journey from home on Saturday, when the Manchester Free Wanderers were met at Fallowfield. Previous encounters have always been decided at Wilderspool, frost or some other unavoidable circumstance preventing the meeting on the Manchester club's ground. However, fortune favoured the Wanderers with a splendid day on Saturday, and the greater portion of the small muster of spectators who witnessed the encounter journeyed from Warring- ton.

Both teams were strong, and punctiral to the advertised time. Anderton started operations, Evans meeting a kick off with a grand return to the Wanderers' quarter flag. From a pack at the Free Wanderers' twenty-five, Turner came through until his career was checked by a smart save on the part of Oswald. Danger threatened the Manchester goal, until a smart dribble by the Wanderers' skippe—Anderton—removed hostilities to half way. Povey pressed the home team back to their lines. Walker and Evazis each showed up for their respective sides, but neat passing by Antrobus and imeakman took the oval to the line. Nevins endeavounld to score with a tricky run, but his pass was intercepted by Hindle, who transferred the game to the quarter-flag. The Wanderers tried hard to invade the Warrington quarters, but all to no purpose, for a smart run by Sireakman almost had the desired enect, McColl eventually conceding a minor.. The drop-out found play well in the Manchester quarters, Barnes putting in some grand work, and almost got in after a good run being pushed into touch close to the line. Schofield run, the pressure with a smart run, but Speakman, Antrobus, and Evans treatei the lookers- on to a good display of passing, taking the ball from midfield to the home team quarter flag. Barnes made another effort, but again danger was averted. Speak- man and Antrobus again put in some short passing, and a strong kick by Barnes again forced the Wanderers to save. A grand return to the drop out by Antrobus placed Warrington on the aggressive, but a smart dribble by Anderton was ably neutralized by similar tactics on the part of Ashton. Barnes made an extra effort here, and a drop at goal by Evans was charged down in the nick of time. Massey added another minor to the Warrington score. The restarting found the Man- chester representatives invading the Warringtonground, and after some give-and-take play Anderton and McClure nere the means of taking the oval to the War- rington lilies. Antrobus.started a movement which was taken up by Barnes at hi 4 quarter flag, and picking up in splendid style he dodged his opponents In a remark- able manner, and finally scored as brilliant a try as ever was secured, the same player placing a neat goal. From the re-starting Anderton played a prominent part, but no addition was made to the score, half-time arriving with the score.—Warrington, one goal, three minors to Free Wanderers nil. Resuming hostilities from midfield Evans essayed to cross the line. but McColl held him. Speakman and Antrobus put in tricky work, placing the home team in their quarters. Massey and Hindle ex- changed kicks, until a drop at goal by Oswald forced a minor. Kennedy put in neat work, until a spirited run by Massey eventually ended in a minor being added to , the visitors' score. Forward play was now indulged in until Turner, Ashton, and Povey, dribbled neatly to the Manchester line. McColl and Kennedy passed neatly, but the last named was baulked before he could make headway, Turner staying his career. The Warrington forwards were now playing with renewed vigor, and were having a deal the best of the game. A kick by Massey was touched in its; career by one of the home team, and the visitors follow- ing up in smart style E. Dillon got over, but on appeal this was disallowed. Evans ought to have scored here, but through his eagerness lost a golden opportunity. Nevins soon after showed up with a strong run to the Manchester line, and succeeded short- ly after in getting over, but again the ball had to be called back. Antrobus and Evans compelled Holt to save, but a fush by the Warrington forwards was taken over the line, W. Dillon being the lucky recipient, Barnes adding another goal. Only minor points were added, and eventually time was called, Warrington gaining their sixth successive victory by two goals six minors to Free Wanderers one minor.

The game was chiefly forward, and in this department as well as in the back division Warrington were far superior to their opponents. Barnes was the best of the three-quarters, and certainly has not been seen to better advantage this season. Evans. was rather selfish at centre, and it is to be hoped this fault will soon be remedied. The halves passed smartly, their tricky play being greatly, admired. All the forwards played well, and it was pleasing to notice the re-appearance of the dash which characterized their play of last season. On the Wanderers' side, Anderton, Muffle, and Kennedy were for choice.

The following were the teams :—Warrington: T. Jolley, back; T. Barnes, J. W. Evans, and J. T. Massey, three-quarter backs; W. Speakman and W. Antrobus, half backs; if. Ashton, Fair Turner, W. Povey, R. Littlewood, E. Dillon, W. Handles, W. Nevins, T. Cr eag- han, and W. Dillon (captain). forwards. Free Wan- derers: H. Holt, back; T. Hindle, H. McColl, and F. Kennedy, three-quarter backs; I. Oswald and E. C. Holt, half backs; C. Anderton, W. Schofield, J. Worth- ington, F. Walker, C. E. Walker, E. McClure, J. Taylor, A. Erskine, and A. K. Damn, forwards. ,

The New Zealanders continued their tour on Saturday at Birmingham. where they met the Moseley team. The game, which was witnessed by five thousand spectators, was an exciting one, and resulted in the victory of the home players, who obtained two gaols, the Maoris get- ting one gaol and a try. At half-time the Moseley men led by two goals to one; and the only point gained in the second half was the try for the Maoris. The representatives of the Warrington premier foot- ball club again won a double victory on Saturday, the ' first team beating the Free Wanderers on their own ground, and the "A" team simply annihilating the second string of the Wanderers on the Wilderspool ground. This is the first time this season that Warring- ton spectators have had an opportunity. of seeing the "A" team at work and they turned up in considerable force. The game was not a model one from an on- looker's point of view simply because it was one-sided. Enough was seen, however, to convince any one that the local players are keeping up, and even improving upon, the high standard they reached last season. The passing which is carried on systematically was always good, and all the players, both backs and for- wards, show that dash and alertness which are the best guarantee of victory. It will take a strong set of oppo- nents to lower the colours of Adamson'sfollewers if they keep up Saturday's combination. The Canadian football team on Wednesday played a drawn game with the University of Oxford, one goal being scored on each side. Runcorn Club had a very hard task set them on Saturday. The county robbed the team of five of the best players to take part in the trial match at Stock- port, and, thus weakened, they journeyed to Burton-on- Trent to meet the champions of the Midlands. Matters were rendered worse through the fact that Cawley was unable to take Davie's place at three-quarter in conse- quence of illness, and that "Pat" Woods gave his injured vanity a chance by declining to act as substi- tute for Brazendale at the eleventh hour. If the Committee do their duty to the club, they will know how to deal with such insubordination, which is directly opposed to the true inter,* of sport. . . • ..

Notwithstariding these drawbacks, Runcorn gave their opponents a fine, open game, and eventually won in handsome style. A good impression was made upon the Burton folk, who cheered the wearers of the green to the echo, and the fixture will no doubt be an annual one.

The five players engaged at Stockport distinguished themselves. No less than four scored tries, and the ,fifth, Brazendale, was within an ace of doing the same trick. Their places in the county tpartl are assured. On Saturday, Widnes placed their best available team in the field against Oldham, and won a hard game in good st le. Plumpton, the captain, was in his usual place, and exhibited grand form, putting in several capita runs. Hopes are entertained that, if he keeps up to his present level, he will be awarded county honours before the season is over.

When I look further amongst the faces on the wall, a sorrowful feeling canes over me, as I think how busy death has been mowing away with his scythe. Dear Mr. Pilcher, a good friend of mine, gone to the other side. Near twelve months has now elapsed since I and my family left the old town, yet, in so short a time, how many I prominent figures has Warrington lost! • I always glance through the report of the Town Council's proceedings, because I expect to see the free lance of Councillor Bolton prodding either friend or foe. I have his counterfeit presentment looking down towards me,and I think of his auriculas, and his tomatoes. I think with the former he would be the boss here; with the latter he would ' be nowhere. For a shilling,l can get a barrowful of " tommy-toes." There is yet another picture on the wall, the face on 'which I never knew, and yet it takes me . brick to the kindly face of Mr. Haynes and his shoe store in Horsemarket-st. Although only a Christmas almanack, it takes me back to the time of hand-shaking and good wishes. In the corner there • is another small picture, medallion shape, a kind of smiling face is that. Warrington's truest friend, one who in his kindness knows no party: Thankful am I. • that, in ever having the opportunity of voting for Mr. McMinnies, I voted for one of England's truest sons, and one of Ireland's best friends. Long may he live, and may good health be his in abundance 1 Other faces there are on the walls; four there in a group, names not to be mentioned, I suppose. Adjoining there is anotik, group of three ladies; the whole seven, friends with whom I passed my last hours in England; friends with whom I hope to pass my first hours should I ever return, say—to assist at the opening of the Ship Canal. I think the first bit of home-sickness I felt was when I received these very successful efforts of Mr. Birtles' art. But let that pass, I wish to speak a word of the Ship Canal. How strange that I, almost the first to move the question in Warrington, in these later developments should be here in" far Cathay" and should neither see the first sod hinted nor have the intense pleasure of seeing the labour-saving German and American navvies. Well, if I cannot see the wonder- ful changes going on around Warrington in reality, I can see them on paper, thanks to the "Ship Canal News." Some of the illustrations are really things of beauty for woodcuts, notably the one showing, the Pickering Arms at Thelwall. Many a time have lin this hostelry discussed the probabilities of the Ship Canal movement ever getting through its 'initial stages, , and now, Mr. 'Wright, the boniface

presiding at this country-side ale-house. may drink my good health, at his own expense, and remember me to a few of his friends when talking of the changes to which their quiet country-side is being sub- jected. Well, this talk about faces must cceßie to a close, but not before I say that there are three or four more that I want, and which I hope to get. I propose, shortly, to place with Mr. liirtles a few photos of views in this district ; also of various members of my family, so that friends and acquain- tances may see samples of the photographic art in this land of sunshine and fleas. Sept. 26th 1888. [We intend te reprint in our next issue the letter referred to by our esteemed Correspondent. —ED. Ex.]
BANKRUPTCY OF A WARRINGTON BUTCHER.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, yesterday morning, before Mr. A. B. Potter, the assistant Official Receiver, Alfred Bowcock, butcher, Bridge-st., came up for his first examination in bankruptcy. In his statement to the Official Receiver the debtor attributed his failure tq want of capital. He commenced business in 1875 with- out any capital,as a butcher, at his present premises, 80, Bridge-st., Warrington. He had never had any capital. In explanation of a deficiency of £193 14s. 10d, the bankrupt filed the following statement :—" Excess of liabilities over assets on the Ist day of March, 1885, £7O ; expenses incurred since theist day of March, 1885, other than usual trade expenses, namely house- hold expenses of self and wife and three children have amounted to more than the profits made in my business since the above date by the sum of £123 its. 10d." This deficiency account, the Official , Receiver said in his stanement, was extremely` unsatis- factory, but, owing to the absence of proper books, he did not see that the bankrupt could give any better explanation. ,As the matter stood, he had apparently been living on his creditors, at any rate for the last twelve months. It was obvious that he ought to have filed his petition long ago, and it was ridiculous of him to assert that he was only aware of his insolvency last March. The bankrupt appeared to have kept cash books recording his receipts and payments up to the 24th July, 1884 ; from that time to the 4th of July, 1888, there was no record. Upon the 4th July, 1888, he recommenced entering his cash, and continued to do so until the 22nd Sept. His books did not show his financial position at any time, no entry being made of purchases on credit, ol• any other liability. He admitted tat he had not within the last three years prepared any statement of his affairs ; that he never took stock, and that he had no accounts showing his income, aid household and:personal expenditure, during the last three years. In March, 1885, he called a private meeting of his creditors, most of whom accepted a comppsition of 10s. in the £. The rest he paid in full. His liabilities then were about £lOO. After a number of questions had been put to, and answered by, the bankrupt, the exam- ination was adjourned until the 30th of next month.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

itIOORE TO STOCKTON HEATH. The favourable weather of the last week has been taken full advantage of by the agents for the Moore and Acton Grange Sections, and to replace the work done by the night shifts, the men in some parts have made longer days. The winter period of inactivity is thus kept off as long as possible. At Acton Grange the new Mission Hall was opened on Sunday. There was a good attendance and the new minister preached. A descrip- tion of the hall was given in our columns last week. At Walton, progress is necessarily slow on account of the hard rock which is being cut through at present. At that part of the works which is situated at Stockton Heath, the most noticeeble advance is in the making of the new road. DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD AND THE SHIP CANAL. At a meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board, on Thursday, it was mentioned that the east road at the village of Lower Walton, which ran across the course of the canal, had been bridged over so as to allow for the passage of vehicles, in accordance with a temporary agreement entered into by a Committee appointed by the Board and the contractor. This agreement was adopted by the Board. Mr. T. S. Burgess mentioned that another road near Lower Walton had been broken up by the canal contractor without first having obtained the sanction of the Board. He (Mr. Burgess) supposed that this had been done in mistake, as the road was very little used,and probably the contractor had not expected that it was a highway under the jurisdiction of the Board. One or two members thought that interference with roads without the consent of the Board was an irregular proceeding that ought not to be all ,wed. Mr. P. W. Long said tha, unless they wished to stand in the way of that great work, from which they all hoped so much for the district, they must either give some one temporary authority in matters of this kind,or else meet oftener than every three months. (Hear, hear.)—lt was ultimately agreed that a standing Committee consisting of the following, viz. :—Messrs. Cooper, Bradford, Beswick, Darbyshire, Parr, and Jones, should be appointed, together with the Surveyor, to confer with the canal contractor when the need arose.—An applica- tion was read from Mr. Prouse, engineer at the Latch- ford section of the canal (who was in attendance) for the Board's sanction to remove the level crossings of the branch lino, on Grapp9nhall-road, and Knutsford-road, nearer the level crossings of the London and North- Western Railway Company. This permission was granted.—Mr. W. Long referred to the diversion of Thelwall-read, and said that the new road almeared to be very well laid though it was rather heavy as yet owing to the amount of loose macadam upon it. A SUCCESSFUL CANAL. All who are interested in the Manchester Ship Canal enterprise may be encouraged by the results of the canalisation of the Main up to Frankfort. It is just two years since the new navigation was opened, and the results have already surpassed all expectations. During last year the traffic amounted to 15,500,000 tons trans- ported one kilometre. Against the average for 1880-2, this shows an increase 49-fold; and against 1878, 60-fold. The total movement of merchandise to and from Frank- fort (that is, without taking into account the distance) averaged 1,050,000 tons per annum during 1884-8. Of this total, 897,000 tons were transported by rail and 152,000 tons by water. Last year the total movement was 1,373,000 tons, the quantity by rail being 1,013,000 tons and by water 360,000 tons. Thus the railways have apparently benefited by the increase of traffic induced by the canalisation of the river ; at the same time the traffic by water has increased from a proportion of 14 per cent. of the total to a proportion of 26 per cent. The increase in the movement by rail is 36 per cent. and by water 64 per cent. These figures, it is stated, do not includegoods in transit merely, or the timber rafts. Adding these, the movement by water would be increased to 654,000 tons last year. In the course of a single year Frankfort, which formerly relied mainly on its financial business, and which has in recent years suffered in this respect from the competition of Berlin as a monetary and stock and share market, has become a serious competitor as a commercial centre with all the Rhine ports. The total coal movement at Frankfort has increased 42 per cent., the figures being last year 387,000 tons, against 259,0013 tons. This increase has been entirely by water, the coal transport by water having increased from 4,790 tons to 157,020 tons; meanwhile the movement of coal by rail has declined 17 per cent., from 254,000 one to 210,000 tons. It is calculated that the saving to consumersl which has resulted from the change to water carriage on zza! alone amNnttd to £20,000 last year. Last year 31,000 tons of wheat Ikeie èâs io Pr4llllf Ott by water, against 1,261 tons in 1888; 9,963 tons of rye, against 2,066 tons. The Raving on the rates for grain in conse- quence of the canalisa ion of the Main is estimated at 1 Tait q'jpi. per ton, which, it is pointed out, to some extent off-sets the import duty. The traffic is increasing again this year. lost year the movement of the port of Frankfort bys the canalised portion of the Main exclusive- ly was 250,000 tons. For the first six months of 1888 it amounted to 200,000 tons, and it is expected that the total for the year will be from 400,000 to 500,000 tons, OETs.TERAJ.4 PROGRESS. Now that the season of comparative inactivity on works of the character of the Manchester Ship Carol , is at hand, a brief review of the progress made on that ' undertaking since the first sod was cut at Eastham, a little less than 12 months ago, will be of general interest. So vast is the magnitude of the enterprise, and so for- I midable are some of the engineering difficulties to be overcome, that works which in the ordinary run of things would be regarded as considerable, pass merely as ordinary incidents. For the sake of continuous working the 35 miles odd of the canal line have been divided into some eight or nine sections, upon the whole of which more or I,ns work is being done. The most active sections at present are at the extreme ends—at Posthorn, where the debonchernent into the Mersey is to take p.lace; and at Salford, where the basins and docks are in full piogiess. The least effort has yet been shown 'en Considerable stretch between the furthest point yet 'reached on the Eastham section, which includes the paSSlng of Ellesmere port, and a long line of embank- rnents where the canal encroaches on the existing bed of the river, and the whole of the westerly part of the Runcorn section from the Weaver river to beyond Run- corn Bridge over the whole of which distance the Canal will be formed in the bed of the Mersey, skirting close by the existing sea wall of the Weston Canal and the Weston 'and Runcorn Docks. On this long and important stretch nothing has yet been done beyond the collecting of enormous stacks of piles and other materials. After getting past Runcorn there is a scene of almost continuous activity for a stretch of many miles, in- cluding the Norton, Acton Grange, Latchford, and Warburton sections or sub-sections, the whole having a line of rail intercommunication. In the neighbourhood of Warrington, and again at Irlam, the serious task of passing under the railways has to be faced, and this, of course, can only be done by making deviation lines, and carrying them over by means of embankments and bridges at vastly higher elevations than at present. The embankments are being made at various points, and form a convenient mode of disposing of portions of the excavated matter. The canal, of course, preserves as straight a line as possible, the only formidable curve being round Weston Point. The rivers Mersey and Irwell, however,above Warrington, twist and wind very much, and the canal has to cross them so repeatedly that at or about the point where the river becomes tidal, and thence on to the terminus, the canal practically takes the place of the rivers, an elaborate sluice ar- rangement controlling all storm waters. From a deep stone cutting at Warburton up to Barton, the engineer- big troubles, excepting the river crossings, are of the slightest, but when Barton village is reached they accumulate with startling rapidity ; a large weir in the river itself, a roadway, and, most formidable of all, the Bridgewater Canal, all crossing the line of the Ship Canal within a distance of about 50 yards. The canal is to be carried over by the unique device of a swing aqueduct, and as the traffic on the Bridgewater Canal is very considerable the experiment will be one of great interest. On this half mile or so nothing has yet been done beyond the laying of a line of rails under the Barton Bridge, and supported on piles in the bed of the river. From this point, however, up to Trafford-road, Manchester, the activity is very great, and rightly so in proportion to the immense volume of work here to be done, for not only is the width of the canal to be extended by 30ft. from Barton to Manchester, a distance of fully three miles, but at Manchester and Salford end more than 100 acres of dock space have to be excavated. Good progress has been made up to Throstle Nest Weir and the surface has just been broken beyond, but the Manchester docks proper, as dis- tinguished from those of Salford, where considerable progress is made, have not yet been commenced. Broadly gauging the result so far, from a careful inspec- tion, the conclusion must be that in the mere work of excavation, enormous though that is, the contractor is well up to time, but the constructive works to be done and not yet touched are so numerous and ticklish in character that, if the works are to be completed in something less than 39 months from this date, the feat will certainly be the smartest in engineering records. THE NAVVIES AND THEIR DRINKING HUTS. At the Chester County Petty Sessions, held at Chester Castle, on Saturday, the magistrates were engaged some hours in hearing charges against several hut keepers on the Ship Canal works at Ellesmere Port, of selling beer by retail without licenses. The defendants were Peter Bond, Elias Mortimer, Joseph Johnson, George Griffiths, George Diamond, John Tyrrell, and Martin Perritt ; and the offences were alleged to have been committed 0 between the 23rd and 30th of last month. Mr. W. H. Churton, solicitor, Chester, appeared to prosecute on behalf of the police. Mr. Se.gar, barrister, Liverpool, defended Bond, Mortimer, Griffiths, and Diamond; and Mr. Brassey was for the other defendants.—For the prosecution, Mr. Churton stated that Tyrrell was sum- moned for three separate offences of selling beer at a hut at Ellesmere Port without having first obtained a license. on the 23rd, 24th, and 30th ult. A number of huts had been erected for the accommodation of the Ship Canal navvies at the Port, and the police received information that the buildings were being used for illicit drinking by the men on the works. Consequently the Chief Con- stable (Cot. Hamersley) instructed two officers named Hough and William Thomas, to proceed to Elles- mere Port, on Sunday, 23rd September, and they obtained employment on the Ship Canal

the following day. After the t elice • had been there some little time a search warrant was issued, and amongst others Tyrrell's place was searched, when there was found in the hut two eighteen-gallon casks of ale full and untapped, and another on tap.—Williams and Hough deposed to being supplied with pints of ale at a strange navvy's orders on payment.—Mr. Brassey said his client desired him to admit the offence, and a.sked the Bench to deal leniently with him. The fact was defendant had been a lodging- house keeper in Liverpool for over twelve years, and had carried on the business during the whole of that time without a single complaint againstijiim and when, unfortunately, he opened this large plrEeat Elle.smere Port, where he had accommodation for 120 navvies who would not submit patiently to be supplied with drink Ito their dinner brought from a distance of three-quarters of a mile or thereabouts, heentertained the idea of gett- ing the beer to supply his lodgers, and he accordingly enteredinto it. Defendant commenctd the beer-selling some six weeks ago.—ln Bond's csse the facts were simi- lar. An eighteen-gallon. cask of beer was found in the bedroom on a stiilage.—Elizabeth Bond said that the hut was her property and under her control. She always kept a barrel of beer in the house, because she liked a glass, aad so did the lodgers.—William Cuff, a lodger, said he paid 15s. per week for his board and lodging, and two pints of beer per day were allowed, These were the terms all the lodgers lived on. Theever got as much beer as they liked.—After a short deliberation, the magis- trates fined Tyrrel and Bond £lO and costs each. Mr. .Brassev appeared for the defence of Joseph Johnson, charged with three similar offences at Whitby, on the 26th, 28th, and 29th ult. Defendant pleaded guilty, and the bench imposed a similar penalty of £lO and costs. Elias Mortimer was summoned for a like offence.—Police- constable Hough proved the case, and defendant was fined £lO and costs.—The Chairman reminded defendant that distress would be levied in default, and if insufficient defendant would have to go to prison for two months hard labour. Martin Perritt, was charged with a similar offence, and Mr. Brassey defended. An 18-gallon barrel of beer, two half-barrels of beer, and another full half- barrel, in a separate part of the house, were found by the police, and Hough was served.—The offence was denied ;though defendant in cross examination, admitted having been fined £2.5 and £lO for the same offence at Penarth : and Mr. Churton said he had instructions that the defendant was on the Ist inst. again fined £2.5 at Penarth for illegal liquor selling.—The Chairman said this was far the worst case of all, and the sentence of the court was a fine of £2.5 and costs, or two month's imprisonment. George Diamond, another hut proprie-' tor, was similarly charged with illegal liquor traffic, Mr. Churton prosecuting, and Mr. Segar defended.—Fined £lO and costs, or two months' imprisonment. George Griffiths, a hut proprietor, was also summoned fora similar offence, and was mulcted in a penalty of £lO and costs.

div.head: HARRY SPEAKMAN IN AI7BTRALIA, AMONGST RUNCORN FRIENDS. THE DEATH OF THE, CAPTAIN.
div.p: HARRY SPEAKMAN IN AI7BTRALIA, AMONGST RUNCORN FRIENDS. THE DEATH OF THE, CAPTAIN.

(Concluded.) On Saturday I went round toseemy friends. Here is G. Riley. that formerly worked for Mr. Leach, the tailor. He lives at Paddington—two miles from Sydney, and I paid him a visit. In the afternoon °lir team met Sydney University, and I again occu- pied the half-back position. We won by 8 points to 4. There were 6,000 spectators. At night we Went to Foley's Boxing Class to see a match for a cup worth .E5O, but the slugging only lasted six minutes. Sunday, the twelfth, I spent with Riley. We went to chapel to hear" a service of song, and afterwards I went to one of Riley's friends for tea. We spent the night siaging hymns. I started for home at ten. [The letter then describes the journey to Maitland,and the fun the team had there, "Tommy Nolan" upsetting Torn Banks in the river, while the latter was having a row in a skiff.] After the lunch, we started for Newcastle, but left J. Anderton, A. E. St,oddart, and Bob Seddon behind, as ' they were going to have a sail. When we arrived at Newcastle, we were told that Seddon, our captain, was drowned, and alas! the news was too true. We passed the night in sorrow. We cancelled the game on the morrow, and returned to Maitland. Seddon was lying in a coffin at the Royal Hotel, and thousands of folk came to see him. There were some splendid wreaths placed on his coffin by ladies for his mother's sake. We laid him in his last resting place in the cemetery ; and there was not a man amongst us whose heart was not filled with sorrow when we had to leave forever a cap- tain with whom we had all been so familiar day after day. In the evening we went to a meeting, for the folks to his memory before we wanted to erect something left the country. There was over £3O got in an hour. At twelve that night we left for Brisbane, and the first man I met there on my arrival atter a weary journey, was the old captain of the Runcorn te,att—Forrie Bate. I was very glad to see him, or anybody else from our town. He was looking well, and he told me he was doing well. The 'earn was received by the Mayor of the town, who expressed great sorrow at the death of L. Seddon. We made A. E. Stoedirt ettptsin of the team, and he spoke very nicely, but tears came into his eyes while he said he was taking the place of one that we all had loved so much. After tea was over I was met by Ted Wright. He is doing very well, I can tell you, and is well respected by all that know him here. He invited me to his house for the night. Next day we were all ready to play the game with the Northern team. We won easily by 13 points to 7. I was •playing half back. I got two tries, and am playing very well in that position. After this we were taken t o see the Run of Luck at the Royal Theatre, and after- wards retired to bed at 12 o'clock. The folk here are a good sort ; the best I have met yet. On Sunday, the 19th, .I was up early, and went to church with Paul, and after lunch went to the hospital to'see G. Bent, who was lying there after an accident.' I found he was recovering very fast, but the doctor said he would be well looked after if we left him there. It was very hot just then, about 80 in the shade. We came back to our hotel to sit on the verandah. It is most enjoyable here in the shade at night. Afterwards I and Tom Haslem went to church again. I never miss, if well. On Monday, the 20th,we were taken to the Baths, and afterwards round the town. Aft3r dinner Ted Wright came for me to take me for a drive. On our Way, he took me to see Mr. R. Spofforth. He has alargebutcher's business, and is doing very well. This is the town for anyone to get en who would be steady- During the drive, we had a delightful chatabour the old times in good old Runcorn ; and had many a laugh at the rem- embrance of things that had happened to us. He is just the same as he wasinßuncorn,and is now a Majorin the Salvation Army. He has a fine house, and keeps a trap , to ride about in. I returned to the hotelfor dinner, as I ' had an engagement to go to a skating rink that night,. and a jolly time I spent there, finishing up with an oyster supper. The next day I penned a letter to my mother, and afterwards played in a match with 18 Juniors, and beat them 23 to 5. After the match I wasintroduced to Mrs. Spofforth, whom I had not seen before. I was up early on the 22nd, and went down the har- bour for a sail with the representatives of the Rugby Union. This I enjoyed, and afterwards went to Ted Wright's for tea. I called for him at his office, and drove out with him, calling on the way for Mrs. Spof- forth. After tea Mr. Spofforth came up, and we passed the whole of the night talking about Runcorn. I forgot to say I was introduced to Ted's wife to-night,and a very nice lady she is When we came to leave at night, I essayed to mount Mr. Spofforth's horse, and all went well for a time, when suddenly the saddle shifted, and let me down very quietly into the dust. Otkmy way home, I called to see some of our men who, with myself, had been invited to a dance, but I did not remain, as I wished to be in form for the coming Thursday. The next morning I was astir early, and we left by train for Ipswich, about an hour's drive from here, where we were to play a match We were met at the station by the Mayor, and taken for a drive round the town, after which we had lunch. The people here are principally Irish, and very nice people tea, and would do anything for us. The match ended in a win for us by 11 to 1, and we spent the night at a smoking concert. When we came to leave by train at night, we found the station besieged by the townsfolk who had come to see us off. The next morning I found my arm very sore, having hurt it on the ground, which is very hard here. In fact, if it was not so! think we could play every day. I went to the Baths for a swim, and afterwards took a stroll round the town; and in my rambles came across a turtle that had just been caught,and weighed 390 lbs. After dinner, the whole team went to a ball, where I stayed until 3 next morning. After breakfast the next morning, I went for a walk in the town, and met Forrie Bate, and afterwa.rdsgot ready for the match to be played that day, which we won by 7 points to nil. It was a good game, but rough, most of our men getting hurt. I myself got a beauty of a black eye. On the 26th I was up at nine, and went to Mr. Spoff- orth's for the day. I had a walk round his premises. He has fine horses and a great quantity of live stock, and he is doing a good business. After dinner we had company, and I spent a pleasant evening amongst Mr. Spofforth's friends, many of whom came because I was there. When I left this place, they all came to see me off at the station, and I was given a splendid match box made out of a curious nut only grown in Queensland. We travelledto Newcastle—in sleeping cars—and on the 29th we were ready. for the game with the team of that place. It was blowing very hard. We won by 13 points to seven. I got two tries. I was playing centre three- quarters again. Stoddart is hurt with a bad shoulder. We go to-night for Sydney at 1.30, and on the 30th we sail for New Zealand, where we play Auckland, &c. We sail for home on the 6th of October, when I hope to see all welLagain after our jolly tour. The letter concludes with kind regards to numerous friends and acquaintances.
Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's, which for strength is unegualled.—dtdvt.

div.head: MR. LUKE FILDES, R.A.
div.p: MR. LUKE FILDES, R.A.

Through the courtesy of Mr. Francis George Heath, the Editor of "Illustrations"—an admirable threepenny fine art journal—we are enabled to place before our readers the above portrait of Mr. Luke Fildes, R.A., one of several eminent artists who were in early life connected with the Warring- ton School of Art. Mr. Fildes is of Lancashire birth, having, we believe, first seen the light in the neighbourhood of Liverpool. Very soon in life, however, he went to Chester where he lived with a grandmother, and in his early teens he became a student in the School of Art in that ancient city. While acting as an art pupil teacher at Chester school, his artistic abilities seem to have attracted the attention of the art in- spector. Mr. R. G. Wyk", who, thinking ,he would have much better chanees of learning more advanced branches of the art in which he dcsired to become proficient at Warrington, recommended him to Mr. J. C. Thompson, who was then and until three or four years ago,the head master of Warring- ton School of Art. The result of this recommend- ation was that in 1861 or 1862 Mr. Fildes removed to Warrington, and pursued his studies there under the supervision of Mr. Thompson. About that time Warrington school held a singularly high position amongst provincial Schools of Art, and we find on referring tq an official pamphet published in 1867, that in 1861 the Warrington school obtained the full- compliment of local medals .(30) and five medallions in he succeeding national cotnpetition, Birmingham, with its 902 students, against War- rington's 147, was the 041 y other provincial school out of 85 competing l*hich obtained the same number. The school was also prolific of able scholars, and Mr. Fildes had as fellow students Mr. 11. Woods and Mr. Brewtnall, both of whom, like himself, have since won high positions in the world of art. While'in Warrington. Mr. Fildes won two national medallions, and a national scholarship, this latter enabling him to study at South Kensington Training School, and we believe Mr. H. Woods, who was also the winner of a national scholarship, went up to South Kensington in the same year. With his departure to South Kensington—which took place, we e, in 1863--Mr. Fildes terminated a connection with Warrington which was, we cannot but think, both useful to himself, and creditable to our local school‘of art and its headmaster.
A f.nv weeks ago a well-written article by Mr. M H. Spielman, appeared in the "Graphic," from which we give some extracts.
EARLY SUCCPSS.

It is not without reason. says Mr. Spielman. that Mr. LukeFildes is oftenlooked upon as the enfant "ydteof the Royal Academy. A man hardly destined to know what disappointment is, he early fdund the ladder to fame and fortune (as the conventional figure runs) set before him, and he calmly walked straight up it, till he now finds himself somewhere very near the top. He certainly occupies a very enviable position in the world of Art, for, beginning by laying the public under a debt of gratitude for the pathetic, heart-chastening pictures be placed before it—and, after allithere is ufithin„.. the public loves so well as to have RI heart chastened—he now extorts its ready applause with the gay harmonies ,4 colour and the bngbt. scenes of happy and. pictures- que Venetian life with which he enlivens the walls of Burlington House, All ARTIST'S RESIDENCE. tie WIS 'hardly thirty-three when he was enabled to build the beautiful house ll cupiefs ipl4lllPrYl4:--,-• that "posy of artists' dwellings" with so many of his fellow-members as neighbours. Indeed, police permit- ting, he could without undue exertion throw stones into the windows of the President, Mr. Watts, Mr. Colin Hunter, Mr. Val Princep, Mr. Thomeycroft, Mr. Marcus S one, and Mr. Richmond. His own house, one of Mr. Norman Shaw's best "examples," bears comparison with any of these for comfort in its arrangements, and beauty and quiet distinction of its decoration, while the charming little garden is unsurpassed among them. The studio, too, is a fine room in which he ornamentation is entirely subordinated to the workshop element. Pannelled in dark oak, it is furnished with the usual luxuries indulged in by a successful painter, but the canvases strewn about on chairs, sofas, and even on the " throne,"proved that here, even more than elsewhere, oil comes to the top. Two peculiarities of the studio consist in the horizontal shutters in the ceiling, with which Mr. Fildes can regulate his top-light to a nicety, and in the large glass-house built out to serve as a winter-studio, where he can take advantage of all the light dark days vouch- safe, with only fogs to baffle him. This is a feature of which I know but one other example—the studio of M. Bouguercau, up a fifth floor in the Rue Notre Dame des Champs.
A " LANCASHIRB .LAD."

Mr. Luke Fildes— is a "Lancashire lad," whose accent betrays his birthplace—a singularly pretty pronuncia- tion purified and beautified by a long residence in Chester, that lends a peculiar Charm to his animated and eloquent conversation. Slim, tall, well-built, and vigorous, he is what men would call " a fine fellow ;" full of natural grace and strength, athletic as becomes a Lancastrian, while there is not a bit of the poseur about him. Indeed, there are few men in a semi- Public position who shrink more completely from the public gaze, and, in truth, it is not without some mis- givings that I commit these impressions to paper. Genial and hearty, honest and outspoken, he bears on his face a tell-taTo expression of refinement and tender- ness that disclose the heart whence came 'The Wid- ower ;" indeed, though I never heard him say so, I'll be sworn that that picture—one of the most tenderly pathetic the present generation has produced—was not Painted without the accompaniment of many a trickling I tear.

YOUTHFUL AMBITION. Left an orphan at a very tender age, young ,Fildes went to take up his abode at Chester under the tutelage of a fond, indulgent, and discerning grandmother. As the boy grew so did his love for the picturesque, and many a sketch did he make of those quaint and lovely "bits" with which the fine old city aboutlds. Through his solicita,inns, he secured the advantage of a drawing- master's instruction—one of the good old orthodox, cast- iron sort—as well as the permission to supplement his ordinary days' schooling with attendances at the local School of Art evening classes. .But, although his ambi- tion did not yet point towards the highest goal, the wall- paper design and oil-cloth-pattern order of instruction did bot quite satisfy the longings of his soul. What he wanted was to draw cows standing in water, overhang- ing trees, and so forth. At last, when he was sixteen years old, he prevailed upon his ever kind grandmother' to allow him for a couple of years to attend the school at Warrington, where" Art for Art" was a more readily- accepted motto than "Art for Floorcloth." To be an artist was still beyond the range of his hopes, and he did not yet feel that the feu mere burned within him. He has told me how the belief that Pictor nascitur, noc ft, would have made him consider it a presumption to say, "I shall be an artist." As he expressed it, in the course of conversation, "becoming an artist" represented to him much the same idea as " coming to the throne."
WOOD-EINDRANING AND " BLACIE-AND-WHITE."

A sight of the International Exhibition of 1862 so fired his enthusiasm that his relative made him an adequate allowance out of her limi,ed store. This enabled him to become a student at South Kensington, and finally at the Royal Academy Schools, where he worked through his "probationary ' period, and duly appeared in "the Life.' But feeling that the time had come when money should be earned, and the burden removed from her who had already spared so much, he did not proceed to learn painting, but sought to draw in black-and-white without delay. With this view he sought out Mr. W. L. Thomas, then" known as one of the foremost wood-engravers in London, submitted his sketch-book as the iaost practical letter of introduction and recommendation, and forth- with obtained employment as a draughtsman on wood— that is to say, as a copyist on the block of other men's work, ready for the engraver; for at that time photo- graphy, on wood was not yet practised. He soon began to try his hand at original illustration, and so strong was his individuality and skill that he speedily worked his way to the front rank of artists in black-and-white This was his real instruction for his painter's career—self- instruction—and he now began that the possibility of which he had hardly dared to hope.
ILLUSTRATES VICTOR H1:760 AND DICKENS.

By I;Z:is of the illustrations to Victor Hugo's "L'Homme qui Rit," to Lever's lost work, and Charles Reade's and Mils Thackeray's books, he conquered a position which placed him side by side with the greatest living artists in black-and-white; and, as chance would have it, Charles Dickens was at that moment on the
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 20, 1888.

watch for an artist to realize the creations in his pro- jected new novel—" Edwin Droell." The novelist had already consulted his friends Mr. Millais and Mr. Frith on the subject, and they promised to keep a look-out. It so happened that "The Graphic" was just then on the stocks, and the proprietors, wishing to make "artis- tic merit," the feature—indeed, it was to be the raison d'être—of the new illustrated paper, wrote to Mr. Fildes I for a drawing. Out came the little book, and the famous "Casuals" drawing was the result. Although I the price demanded was considered very heavy in those days, a request for "as many more as you like at the same mice" was preferred The drawing appeared, and the sensation was tremendous. The same day Sir John Millais hastened down in a cab to Dicken's rooms, and as soon as he came in sight of the house, he waved the first number of "The Graphic" above his head. "I've got him !" he exclaimed, striding into the room. "Got whom 2" "The fellow for " Edwin Drood," he replied, throwing the paper down on the table. No sooner did Dickens examine the plate than hit wrote forthwith to his publishers, who duly communicated with the young artist, stating facts, and asking his terms, at the same time requesting that he should show proof that he could draw " comelfladies." as there was necessarily no evidence of that in the •' Casuals." Mr. Fildes' demands were moderate, his drawings of the female form divine highly acceptable, and everything was satisfactorily settled. The opening designs were soon sent in, and were photographed on the wood; the first examples, I believe, wherein the now constant method was adopted.

AS A PAINTER IN OIL. The death of Charles Dickens threw Mr. Fildes' black- and-white work out of gear, so' to speak, for he had attaintd the highest point in that line, and there Nirere no more worlds to conquer. So he determined to turn his attention to oil-painting—succeeding in such a way that I am, I believe, justified in having described it as phenomenal, under the circumstances. He had never painted in oil Beyond the few studies he had produced in the schoqls, and the efforts he had made a- home by him- self; he had never received any training in this direction, nor given forth anything he thought worthy even of a frame; and he had never seen anybody paint a picture. So it must be conceded that he started without any prejudice. Everthing was tentative and experi- mental ; and yet he stumbled along the right path, and, like Topsy, " growed " unconsciously into a powerful painter; taking to the art naturally, like a duck to water.

A young man, conscientious, earnest, gifted with a bright and sympathetic nature, oj extraordinary power and facility (and blessed with at reasoning ambition to foster and direet them), hardly yet in the heyday of. life and fame, he will assuredly achieve far greater things than he has yet accomplished. He can hardly increase his popularity; but, with his character and his persever- ance, to what excellence may he not attain ? And to what position ?"
RUNCORN LEAGUE OF THE CROSS. _ SPEECH BY FATHER NUGENT.

Under the auspices of the Runcorn branch of the League of the Cross a public meeting was held in Runcorn Public Hall,on Tue,day evening. filers was a capital attendance, tfie building being three- parts filled with an attentive audience. On the platform were the Rev. Father Nugent, of Liver- pool, (founder of the League), Rev. Dr. Gastaldi (chaplain president Runcorn Branch) Rev. Father Chapman, of Widnes • Messrs. J. J. Fitzpatrick, Liverpool. J. P. Bowiand, Liverpool; .1. P. Cullen, manager "Catholic Times," Liverpool ; D. Hough- ton, president Warrington branch; J. Houghton. president Runcorn branch ; Byrne, vice-president; J. Williamson, secretary; N. J. Gordall, .T. Richmond J. Ryan. M. Craig, M. Grimman, J. Quinn, and J. Loughna.

Di Gastaldi, in opening the proceedings, said they were assembled thereithat night for the great purpose of fostering the principles of temperance amongst the people of Runcorn. Re was confident that the meeting would realise the great benefit to be derived by the pres- ence of Father Nugent. (Applause.) His name was known through the whole world as the champion and the great patron of total abstinence,-and his presence would noaioubt give them a further—not only desire, but zeal, for thecause in which they were engaged. He therefore called upon Father Nugent to take the chair and preside over the meetiag. (Applause.) Father Nugen then took the chair amid the enthusias- tic applause of the audience. He thanked them very sincerely for their hearty reception, and Dr. Gastaldi for the very kind words in which he had introduced him. He said he came not to ask their sympathy in a mone- tarvform, but to awaken within them an ihterest in the great work of the League of the Cross. (Applause.) Whatever might be the lines of difference that may separate the people of this thriving town, he felt sure that every right-minded man was glad to see the pro- , gress which the League of the Cross was making in Runcorn. (Applause.) %4 herever we turned, we were appalled with the terrible effect of drunkenness; no day passed without revealing some frightful history springing from this vice, which had got such a hold unon the working classes that no age or sex was free from its ;eteeeee. Those who were listening to him could relate within the narrow sphere oc tneieown lives, what thrrible shipwredo were witnessed day by day amongst young and old—the blighted hopes and prospects of a family dashed for ever. He had rementbered Runcorn for certainly 55 or 58 years. Mimi a mere boy he was in the habit of coming during the summer months to this. neighbourhood. 'then there was no such place as Widnes—no indust* Or smoky chimneys as they saw at present. He asked them to consider how much money had been earned in the industries of Whines during the last 20 years. and, considering the oppor- tunities that the neighbourhood had afforded by its development of industries, and the natural power and genius which must have been exercised, how few men had risen even to an ordinary competency, 'who could compute the amount of money that had been wasted in drink, and the number of families that had been sacrificed. The terrible social evil of drink filled our gaols and workhouses, and drove on to the streets boys and girls to be familiarised at an early period of life with every vice. He asked them as Christain men and women to think of the terrible spiritual de=truction caused by this drink. Drink stripped man of every grace, darkened his reason and understanding, and brought him even to the very level of the beast. If those who were Christians and professed to believe in Jesus Christ, and that He died upon the cross, where was their love, where their faith, if they were not prepared to make some sacrifice in order to stop that terrible cry of sin that rose up to Heaven for justice and judgment? (Applause.) It was within their power, and his, in some measure or other to check this evil. The League of the Cross had been raised up to check and to uproot the power of this vice of intemperance. fl'he League of the Cross VMS not simply an organization composed of those who had been addicted to the sin of intemperance, but it was formed of men and women who in the name and by the power of the Cross voluntarily abstained from the use of drink that they might be an example to others and an organized and combined power to fight both socially and spiritually against the vice of intemperance. (Applause.) The League of the Cross said that the man or woman, who w'as the slave of drink, must, as a necessity, if they sought to overcome that habit, be total ahstamers—no half measures would 'do. (Hear, hear) There had been various organizations which permitted Moderation, but the result of years of patient labour had proved that those who had acquired the habit of drunkenness must not only put the cork in the bottle, but they must break the bottle too. (Applause.) They asked those 71:15 had never been the slaves of drink to Join in this holy warfare, and in the name of God to deny themselves even the little pleasure the sensuous gratifi- cation caused them. He asked the young men and young women to join the ranks of the League of the brass, and to become total abstainers, for there was no necessity for the drink. He asked them as earnest men and women to become volunteers inathe army of the League of the Cross, that by theieself-denial, by the crucifiction of their appetites, and by their example,they could spread abroad the principles of total abstinence and model public opinion against drunkenness, which was undermining the social, moral, and religious condi- tion of the people. (Applause.) Sir William Harcourt recently said at Manchester that they could not make the nation sober by Act of Parliament. But they could lessen the opportunities and protect the people against the degrading and demoralising influence of drink,and it was the bounden du y of Government to protect the people against the dangers that surrounded them. (Applause.) There were acts of Parliament that regulated the chimneys and chemical gases of Widnes. If the Govern- ment was so jealous as to have an act of Parliament to protect the trees and shrubs, and the vineries and the peach-houses, did not they think there ought to be an , act of Parliament, and some vigour of action, to protect ' the morality and well-being of society against the ' dangerous and pestilential influence of the public house. (Applause.) eHe believed Local Option was coming. (Applause.) And it would come all he sooner if they : created a healthy public opinion. They could do this by , not darkening the doors of a publichouse—by having nothing to do with drink, and turning their own hard earned wages to their legitimate and only, purpose—the ' best interests of their families. (Applause.) In conclusion the Chairman urged those present to join the League of the Cross.

The Rev. Father Chapman moved the following resolu- tion: That this meeting, having heard the eloquent address of the Rev. Father Nugent, and recognizing the fearful havoc drink is making amongst all classes of the community, pledges itself to do all in its power to lessen this terrible evil through the organization of the League of the cross." Mr. litzpatrick seconded the motion, which was sup- ported bit Mr. Cullen,tand carried with acclamation. On the proposition of Mr. T. Williamson, seconded by Mr. D. Houghton a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Father Nugent his eloquent address on the prin- ciple of the League ot thd Cross. Father Nugent having responded, administered the pledge lo a considerable portion of the audience, who at his re set knelt down. During the evening the brass band of St. Mary's branch,Warrington, played several selections of popular matude.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board on Guardians was held on Thursday week, at Whiston Workhouse. There were present Mr. J. Kenwright, (chairman), the Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. J. Fisher, W. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson, J Leatherbarrow, W. Middle- hurst, J. W. Waring, R. Ranson, J. Musson, J. Birchall, E. Syder, W. Swift, J. Burchall, E. Birchall, W. Twist, G. Ellison, J. Buckley, J. Lowe, T. Eatock, R. Graves, J. Matthews and S. H. Hartley (clerk.) RE tAev.-4,The Workhouse Master reported there were 523 inmates of the house, against 513 last week, 492 in the corresponding week last year; 58 vagrants had been relieved, against 84 last year. THE APPLICATION FOR AN ADVANCE.—At the meeting of the Finance Committee it was decided to defer the application of Mr. Forster, assistant-overseer, for an increase of salary, until the formation of the new Board. The minutes were passed.

THE WORICHOLYiE EXTENSION.— At the meeting of the Building Committee on the Bth October, Mr. Gandy, architect, produced plans of the proposed extension of the Infectious Diseases Hospital. and for the erection of a Boys' Home, and the same were approved with slight alteration. A deputation was appointed to inspect other Union Offices.—The Rev. Dean Finegan drew attention to the last named minute, and expressed the opinion that their present offices were quite sufficient.—Mr. Leatherbarrow said they had pre- viously passed a resolutien to have new offices.—The Clerk said that was so.—Mr. C. B. Johnson said he had always opposed the erection of new offices and he moved an amendment that the minute in question be referred back.—Mr. Middlehurst thought the deputation was necessary, but he would oppose any extravagant outlay on the new otces.—Mr.E. Birchall seconded the amend- ment, which was lost by 8 votes to 6, and the minutes were then passed. THE VACANCY AT HALEWOOD.—The Local Government Board wrote intimating that they had issued an order for the special election of a Guardian at Halewood in the room of the late Rev. Thomas Chambers.—The Clerk was in- structed to take the necessary steps to bring about the election.

THE WIDNES MEDICAL OFFICER-Mr. Wareing moved in accordance with notice given; the re-appointment of Dr. Cooper as medical officer for the Widnes (lower) Division at a salary of £7O per annum.—The Rev. Dean Finegan seconded, and the motion was passed. This concluded the business.

Mr. Henry Irving laid the memorial-stone on Wednes- day of a new theatre at Bolton. At a banquet held in his honour in the Town Hall he made an interesting speech on the inruence of the drama. By the aid of a dog of the Spitzbergen breed a further discovery was on Wednesday made in connection with the Whitehall mystery. In the vault where the dis- membered body of a woman was found a fortnight ago a human leg was unearthed.

MILL FlRE.—Hollins Mill, Mecklehurst, Mossley, was destroyed by fire on Wednesday night. The building was an old one, but was filled with new machinery. The damage is estimated at about £15,000, and is par- tially covered by insurance. William Waddell was again brought before the magistrates at Durham on Wednesday, charged with the murchn• of Jane 13eetmore, near Gateshead, and was further remanded for a week. The rumour is revived in St. Petersburg that the King of Greece intends to abdicate in favour of the Duke of Sparta af, er the marriage of the latter to the sister of the German Emperor. The German screw steamer Kars, of Hamburg, has been abandoned in the North Sea. The vessel drifted and foundered, but the crew, who had taken to the boats, were picked up by a fishing lugger. According to a Berlin telegram, Major Barttelot fell a victim to the personal malice of a porter, who was delivered up to the authorities at Stanley Falls. Tippoo Tib is said to have been grieved on hearing what had occurred.

The plan adopted by the Prisons Board in Ireland in releasing Father M‘Fadden two days before his sentence had expired in order to prevent a popular demonstra- tion outside the gaol was resorted to again on Wednes- day, when three Milltown Malbay prisoners were dis- charged at Limerick.

NOTICE To QIIIT.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Thomas Foster, agent for some pro- perty at Burtonwood, applied for a notice of eject- ment against James Naylor, occupier of a house and garden. Naylor had been served with a notice to quit but he had not complied therewith. Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, who appeared on his be- half said the reason why Naylor had not left was that he had a valuable stock of celery in the garden and le wiohed to gather it before he left. He would give up the house as he had done so.—The Bench made an order of ejectment in 22 days. ALLEGED EXTENSIVE RAILWAY ROBBERIES.— A GUARD IN InoußLE.—Shem Marsden, assistant passenger guard at Lime-street Station, and who resided at 196, Wavertree-road, was brought up in custody at the Dale-street Police Court, on Friday, charged with stealing a silver lever watch, in transit from Coventry to Prescot, on the 7th March, value .£2 10s.; also with stealing one gentleman's white linen shirt and six collars from a box in transit from Lime-street to Huddersfield on the 21st of July, value 10s. 6d.; likewise with stealing a lady's gold brooch, set in pearl in the centre, out of a tin box whilst in transit from II uyton to Lime- street, on the 11th October; also a quantity of gentlemen's wearing apparel, one pair of 18-caret gold sleeve-links, a silver cigar case, three scarf pins set with stones, &c.—Detective-Inspector Standford said that in consequence of some informa- tion he had received he took the prisoner into his office, and told him he had found some missing articles which he (prisoner) had pledged. Prisoner, after first denyingthat he had tampered with passengers' luggage, subsequently said that he had taken a good many things. On being charged he said, "I am guilty."—.-Prisoner was remanded for seven days. —A gold brooch was found on prisoner, and the police desire to find the owner.

TRAGEDY AT TOTTENITAIL—A sensational tragedy occurred at Tottenham on Wednesday morning. While a man named Thomas Morris, of Waithamstow, was at work in a field, his brother-in-law, Henry Elliott, with whom he had had some unpleasantness about money matters, fired three shots at him with a revolves and then committed suicide. Morris was taken to Tottenham Hospital, where a bullet was extracted from his head and another from his hand.
